capabilities.name: Privacy notice & transparency delivery
capabilities.description: Layered privacy notices and just-in-time transparency UI that surface controller/DPO identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, transfers, retention, and all data-subject rights in plain language for both directly and indirectly collected data, and that flag the right to object explicitly and separately.

stack.name: Transcend (Consent & Preference Management + Privacy Center)
stack.why: API-first platform for a greenfield build that delivers layered + just-in-time notices and hosts a per-user Privacy Center surfacing controller/DPO, purposes, legal basis, recipients, transfers, retention and every data-subject right, with a distinct right-to-object/opt-out control.

stack.name: iubenda
stack.why: Widely-adopted generator that auto-produces and hosts plain-language, layered privacy notices covering all GDPR-mandated disclosures for both directly and indirectly collected data, kept current as processing changes.

stack.name: Klaro!
stack.why: Self-hostable consent/notice widget that renders purpose-level, just-in-time transparency inline at the point of collection — the OSS option when notices must live in your own frontend with no vendor lock-in.

stack.name: Didomi
stack.why: Cross-channel (web, mobile, CTV) preference and notice delivery with geotargeted banners and granular per-purpose controls, letting the right to object be flagged and toggled explicitly and separately from consent.

capabilities.stack_notes: Scope note: this capability is about surfacing/flagging rights (incl. a separate right-to-object control) in the notice UI, not fulfilling DSARs — Transcend/Didomi span both, but the notice-delivery function is what's recommended here. Klaro! covers only the JIT consent/notice UI (no back-office rights orchestration). Other current, comparable managed CMPs: OneTrust, Osano, Usercentrics/Cookiebot. Confirmed current 2025-2026 via web search (ketch.com CMP roundup, osano.com, usercentrics.com).

capabilities.name: Data-subject request intake & access fulfillment
capabilities.description: A DSAR workflow engine that intakes, tracks, and fulfills rights requests within the one-month SLA (with logged extension/decline reasons and complaint-rights messaging), provides free abuse-controlled handling, confirms whether data is processed, and assembles access exports with required metadata and a machine-readable copy that does not expose third parties.

stack.name: Transcend (Privacy Requests / DSR Automation)
stack.why: Automates the full DSR lifecycle — authenticated intake, cross-system data discovery to confirm processing, and assembly of machine-readable access exports — with client-side key management so subject data never traverses vendor infra in plaintext.

stack.name: OneTrust Data Subject Request (DSR) Automation
stack.why: Widely-adopted enterprise intake portal with built-in one-month SLA/deadline clocks, extension and decline reason logging, ID verification and abuse controls, and redaction to avoid exposing third-party data in responses.

stack.name: Temporal
stack.why: Durable workflow engine to model the SLA as first-class code — long-running one-month timers, extension/decline branches, retries, and a fully auditable event history — when you build the intake/tracking engine yourself instead of buying a platform.

stack.name: Osano (Subject Rights Management)
stack.why: Lighter-weight, faster-to-adopt alternative that covers free abuse-controlled intake, request tracking, and complaint-rights/consumer messaging for GDPR/CCPA-style rights without full enterprise data-mapping overhead.

capabilities.stack_notes: Managed platforms (Transcend, OneTrust, Osano) are the pragmatic default for a greenfield build — they ship the intake portal, SLA clocks, extension/decline logging, ID/abuse controls, redaction, and complaint-rights messaging out of the box. Transcend is strongest on actually assembling machine-readable exports via cross-system data discovery; OneTrust is the enterprise standard for intake + workflow + redaction; Osano is the lighter/cheaper option. Temporal is the open-source pick only if you need a bespoke engine — it durably orchestrates the one-month SLA (timers, extensions, declines, auditable state) but you still supply the intake UI, data connectors, and export/redaction logic yourself. Sources: https://www.gartner.com/reviews/market/subject-rights-request-automation , https://transcend.io/blog/dsar , https://my.onetrust.com/s/article/UUID-6d4d8fb4-8c9d-784b-1552-0f5fee9ed5b7 , https://expertinsights.com/compliance/top-data-subject-access-request-dsar-software

capabilities.name: Requester identity verification
capabilities.description: An identity-proofing step in the request pipeline that requires additional identity evidence before disclosing or acting on personal data when there is reasonable doubt about the requester, protecting against impersonated rights requests.

stack.name: Keycloak
stack.why: Mature OSS IAM whose conditional/step-up authentication flows let the request pipeline demand stronger identity assurance (MFA, re-auth) exactly when a requester is doubtful.

stack.name: Persona
stack.why: Widely-adopted IDV orchestration platform for building risk-based document + biometric (selfie/liveness) proofing flows with built-in fraud signals, ideal as the escalation step for high-doubt rights requests.

stack.name: Stripe Identity
stack.why: Drop-in, well-supported government-ID + selfie verification with a simple hosted flow and API, a fast way to collect additional identity evidence before disclosing personal data.

stack.name: Ory Kratos
stack.why: Cloud-native, API-first identity server with MFA and step-up flows, a self-hostable alternative to Keycloak for enforcing elevated assurance inside the request pipeline.

capabilities.stack_notes: The capability spans two layers: (1) step-up authentication to raise identity assurance on reasonable doubt (Keycloak or Ory Kratos), and (2) document/biometric identity proofing to collect fresh evidence (Persona or Stripe Identity). A typical new build pairs one from each layer. All four are current and actively maintained as of 2025-2026 (Onfido, now part of Entrust, is another managed IDV alternative to Persona/Stripe Identity). Confidence is high from domain knowledge; no web search was needed.

capabilities.name: Rectification, erasure & restriction processing
capabilities.description: Data-lifecycle operations that let subjects correct inaccurate data, complete incomplete data with supplementary statements, erase data on qualifying grounds while honoring legal-hold/retention exemptions, and place a reversible processing-restriction state with pre-lift notification.

stack.name: Fides (Ethyca)
stack.why: Privacy-engineering platform whose DSR automation executes erasure and rectification across connected datastores via declarative policies, with masking/skip rules to honor retention and legal-hold exemptions.

stack.name: Temporal
stack.why: Durable workflow engine to model the reversible processing-restriction state as a long-running state machine, gate erasure on legal-hold checks, and fire the scheduled pre-lift notification reliably.

stack.name: Transcend
stack.why: Managed privacy-request orchestration that fans rectification/erasure actions out to first- and third-party systems with audit trails, covering propagation the in-house engine cannot reach directly.

stack.name: OpenFGA
stack.why: Fine-grained authorization store to represent and enforce the restriction/legal-hold flags as relationship tuples, so downstream services can check 'is this subject's data under restriction/hold' before processing.

capabilities.stack_notes: Answered from established knowledge; all four are actively maintained as of 2025-2026. Fides + Temporal form the open-source core (policy-driven data operations plus the reversible-state/notification workflow); Transcend is the managed alternative/complement for cross-system propagation; OpenFGA optionally externalizes the restriction/hold enforcement flag. A team could ship with just Fides + Temporal and add the others as scale/breadth demands.

capabilities.name: Downstream recipient tracking & change propagation
capabilities.description: A recipient/disclosure ledger that records where personal data was shared and, on rectification/erasure/restriction, propagates the change to each recipient (and to other controllers of publicly-disclosed data) unless impossible/disproportionate, and can disclose the recipient list to the subject on request.

stack.name: Fides (Ethyca)
stack.why: Privacy-as-code DSR orchestration engine (Apache-2.0) that maps data flows and fans erasure/rectification/consent changes out to connected databases and third-party apps, and exposes the integration/recipient list — directly implements Art. 19 propagation and Art. 15(1)(c) disclosure.

stack.name: PostgreSQL (append-only disclosure ledger, e.g. via temporal_tables/system-versioning)
stack.why: System-of-record for the recipient/disclosure ledger — an immutable, timestamped log of which recipient received which data on which legal basis, queryable to produce the subject's recipient list and to drive propagation targets.

stack.name: Temporal
stack.why: Durable workflow engine to run the per-recipient fan-out reliably with retries, timeouts and per-recipient status — cleanly models 'propagate to each recipient unless impossible/disproportionate' with an auditable outcome trail.

stack.name: Transcend
stack.why: No-code direct-vendor connectors that automatically propagate erasure/rectification to downstream processors and third parties end-to-end — a managed alternative (or complement) to self-hosting Fides for teams that don't want to run the orchestration engine.

capabilities.stack_notes: Article 19 (notify recipients of rectification/erasure/restriction) + Article 15(1)(c) (disclose recipients to subject) are the governing requirements. Recommended shape: Postgres append-only ledger as the system-of-record, Temporal to guarantee reliable per-recipient propagation with 'impossible/disproportionate' exception outcomes recorded, and Fides as the privacy-as-code engine that maps data and executes DSR fan-out to third-party integrations. Transcend (or OneTrust DSR Automation) is the managed alternative if self-hosting the orchestration isn't desired. Fides and Transcend both confirmed active and expanding erasure/integration coverage as of 2025-2026. Sources: https://www.ethyca.com/fides , https://github.com/ethyca/fides/releases , https://www.onetrust.com/products/data-subject-request-dsr-automation/ , https://temporal.io

capabilities.name: Data portability & structured export
capabilities.description: An export service that outputs subject-provided, automated, consent/contract-based data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, supports direct controller-to-controller transmission where technically feasible, and scopes the export to eligible data without affecting others' rights.

stack.name: Data Transfer Initiative Portability API (formerly Data Transfer Project)
stack.why: The de-facto open standard (backed by Google/Meta/Apple) for direct controller-to-controller transfers in commonly-used, machine-readable formats — covers Article 20's 'transmit directly where technically feasible' clause.

stack.name: Temporal (open-source; Temporal Cloud managed)
stack.why: Durably orchestrates the long-running, resumable export-assembly job — fan-out across services, retries, and scoping to only the subject's eligible data without partial-failure corruption.

stack.name: S3-compatible object storage with presigned expiring URLs (AWS S3 managed / MinIO open-source)
stack.why: Stages the assembled JSON/CSV export bundle and delivers it via time-limited, access-controlled download links so the export self-expires and isn't left exposed.

stack.name: Transcend Data Mapping & DSR automation (or OneTrust)
stack.why: Handles request intake, identity verification, and legal-basis filtering (subject-provided + automated, consent/contract-only) so the export is scoped to eligible data and doesn't affect others' rights.

capabilities.stack_notes: Category: Data Protection (GDPR Art. 20). The DTI Portability API + Temporal + object storage cover a self-built core; the DSR platform (Transcend/OneTrust) is the fastest path to compliant request intake, identity verification, and legal-basis scoping if you don't want to build that layer yourself. For the serialization format itself, standard JSON/CSV (optionally NDJSON for large exports) is the commonly-used machine-readable target — no special tool needed beyond your language's stdlib. Recommendations given from established-tool knowledge; all four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Objection & opt-out management
capabilities.description: A preference/opt-out subsystem that lets subjects object to legitimate-interest/public-task processing and profiling (with a compelling-grounds balancing evaluation), enforces an absolute stop for direct-marketing objections, supports objection to research/statistical processing, and accepts automated machine-readable objection signals.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides
stack.why: Apache-2.0 privacy-engineering framework with a configurable preference center, consent/objection storage, DSR fulfillment workflows, and built-in GPC-signal detection — the strongest open-source base for a subject-facing opt-out subsystem.

stack.name: Transcend Consent & Privacy Requests
stack.why: Middleware layer that captures objections and propagates opt-outs (incl. an absolute direct-marketing stop) downstream to every connected system, with automatic GPC detection and legitimate-interest/objection request handling.

stack.name: Ketch
stack.why: Server-side consent/preference orchestration that enforces opt-outs in real time across CDPs, ad, and AI pipelines and honors GPC natively — good fit where machine-readable signals must halt processing immediately.

stack.name: Global Privacy Control (GPC)
stack.why: The de-facto open browser/HTTP standard for automated machine-readable objection signals (universal opt-out); implement its detection so profiling/sale-and-share objections are honored without a manual step — legally required in 12+ US states as of Jan 2026.

capabilities.stack_notes: The capability spans two proven product categories in 2025-2026: consent/preference management platforms (CMP) and data-subject-rights (DSR) automation — pick one platform (Fides if you want open-source and to self-host the balancing/compelling-grounds workflow, Transcend or Ketch if you want managed downstream enforcement) and layer GPC signal handling on top. The compelling-grounds balancing evaluation for legitimate-interest/public-task and research/statistical objections is a case-management/workflow concern these platforms model as request types but typically require custom review logic; none fully automates the balancing test. Sources: https://github.com/ethyca/fides , https://www.ethyca.com/fides , https://www.ethyca.com/docs/consent/standards/consent-gpc , https://docs.transcend.io/docs/articles/consent-management/concepts/global-privacy-control , https://www.ketch.com/blog/posts/consent-management-platforms , https://www.onetrust.com/blog/global-privacy-control-how-to-honor-consumer-opt-out-requests/

capabilities.name: Automated decision-making & profiling safeguards
capabilities.description: Controls governing solely-automated significant decisions: gating them to permitted grounds (contract, law, or explicit consent), blocking special-category data unless conditions are met, and providing human-intervention, view-expression, and contest mechanisms.

stack.name: Open Policy Agent (OPA)
stack.why: CNCF-graduated policy decision point that evaluates every solely-automated decision inline, gating it to permitted grounds (contract/law/explicit-consent) and denying special-category inputs unless conditions are met.

stack.name: OneTrust (Consent & Preference Management + Privacy Rights Automation)
stack.why: Widely-adopted system of record for explicit consent and lawful basis that OPA/the app checks, and its rights-request intake/fulfillment covers the view-expression and contest channels.

stack.name: Camunda 8
stack.why: BPMN workflow/orchestration engine that routes flagged or contested decisions to human reviewers as user tasks, giving the required human-intervention and contest-handling path with an auditable trail.

stack.name: Fiddler AI
stack.why: Model observability and explainability platform that logs each automated decision and produces per-decision reason/feature attributions, supplying the explanation a data subject needs to meaningfully contest an outcome.

capabilities.stack_notes: Scoped to GDPR Art. 22 (and analogous ADM provisions). Division of labor: OneTrust holds consent/legal-basis + rights intake; OPA enforces the gate and special-category block at decision time; Camunda provides human-in-the-loop review/contest workflow; Fiddler supplies decision logging + explanations for meaningful contest. Camunda and OneTrust also offer managed SaaS; OPA and Fiddler could be substituted by Cerbos (OSS authz) and open-source SHAP respectively if an all-OSS stack is preferred. All four are current and actively supported as of 2026; no web search was needed given their maturity.

capabilities.name: Lawful-basis & purpose governance
capabilities.description: A processing registry that binds every activity to an identified lawful basis before it begins, records legitimate-interests balancing, enforces fair processing, purpose limitation, and a compatibility assessment for further use, gates criminal-conviction data to official-authority conditions, and ensures any restriction of data-subject rights rests on a lawful, necessary, proportionate measure with required safeguards.

stack.name: OneTrust Privacy & Data Governance
stack.why: Market-leading privacy platform providing the Records of Processing (RoPA) registry, built-in legitimate-interests (LIA) and DPIA assessment workflows, and lawful-basis/special-category condition tracking per activity.

stack.name: OpenMetadata
stack.why: Open data catalog with policy-driven classification and tagging to bind each processing activity to the actual data assets it touches and flag criminal-conviction/special-category data, backing purpose limitation and compatibility assessments with real lineage.

stack.name: Open Policy Agent (OPA)
stack.why: Policy-as-code engine to enforce the gate at runtime — deny any processing that lacks an identified lawful basis or falls outside its declared purpose, and encode the necessity/proportionality/safeguard checks for rights restrictions.

stack.name: Transcend
stack.why: Code-first privacy platform (alternative or complement to OneTrust) that models purposes and lawful bases programmatically and propagates them across systems via API, fitting a greenfield build's CI/CD-driven workflow better than a UI-only tool.

capabilities.stack_notes: Roles are deliberately distinct: OneTrust or Transcend owns the registry/assessments (RoPA, LIA, compatibility, Art. 9/10 conditions); OpenMetadata binds activities to classified data assets; OPA enforces the "lawful basis before processing begins" and purpose-limitation gates at runtime. A greenfield 2026 build would pick one privacy platform (Transcend for code-first, OneTrust for breadth) plus OpenMetadata + OPA. All four are current and actively supported as of 2026; confidence is high without web verification given their established market positions.

capabilities.name: Privacy by design & default
capabilities.description: Build-time and runtime measures that embed pseudonymization and data minimization into system design, avoid acquiring or retaining identifying data solely for compliance when identification is not required, and enforce privacy-by-default settings so only data necessary for each purpose is collected, processed, retained, or made accessible without explicit action.

stack.name: Microsoft Presidio
stack.why: Self-hosted PII detection + de-identification (mask/hash/pseudonymize) applied in data pipelines and before logs/analytics/LLM context, so identifying data is stripped by design.

stack.name: Skyflow Data Privacy Vault
stack.why: Isolates PII in a tokenizing vault so apps store/process polymorphic tokens instead of raw identifiers, enforcing pseudonymization and data minimization at the architecture level.

stack.name: OpenFGA
stack.why: CNCF fine-grained (Zanzibar-style) authorization to enforce privacy-by-default access — only the data necessary for each purpose is reachable without an explicit grant.

stack.name: Tonic.ai
stack.why: Generates de-identified/synthetic data for non-production so real identifying data is never acquired or retained where identification isn't required (test/dev/analytics).

capabilities.stack_notes: Piiano Vault is a viable open-source alternative to Skyflow if a self-hosted PII vault is preferred; Gretel (now NVIDIA) is an alternative to Tonic for synthetic data. Presidio + a vault cover pseudonymization/minimization at build+runtime; OpenFGA covers privacy-by-default access; Tonic keeps identifying data out of non-prod. All four verified current as of 2026 via web search.

capabilities.name: Accountability, liability & governance evidence
capabilities.description: Risk-proportionate organizational and technical measures, backed by internal data-protection policies, that demonstrate and evidence compliance with all processing principles, preserve controller/processor-role and lawful-instruction documentation to bound (joint-and-several) liability, and maintain mitigating-factor evidence for fine assessment and national penalty regimes.

stack.name: OneTrust Privacy & Data Governance
stack.why: Market-leading privacy management platform: maintains Records of Processing (RoPA), DPIAs, controller/processor and DPA registers, and generates the audit-ready accountability evidence GDPR Art. 30/24 requires.

stack.name: Fides (Ethyca)
stack.why: Privacy-as-code framework that declares data categories, processing purposes, lawful bases and systems in-repo, producing versioned RoPA and data-map evidence that lives beside the build and stays current via CI.

stack.name: Vanta
stack.why: Continuously collects and timestamps control/policy evidence and manages internal data-protection policies across GDPR/SOC 2/ISO 27001, giving the organizational-measures and mitigating-factor trail auditors and regulators expect.

stack.name: Eramba
stack.why: Open-core GRC system for a risk register, policy lifecycle, and control-to-evidence mapping — a self-hostable backbone for risk-proportionate governance measures and liability-bounding documentation.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. Typical pairing: OneTrust or Fides for the privacy-specific RoPA/DPIA/role documentation, plus Vanta or Eramba as the broader GRC/policy-and-evidence layer. Choose one managed + one open-source depending on data-residency and budget constraints. Drata and Osano are comparable managed alternatives to Vanta/OneTrust if procurement prefers them.

capabilities.name: Encryption & security of processing
capabilities.description: Risk-appropriate technical and organisational security controls — encryption at rest and in transit, pseudonymization, and measures ensuring confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience — protecting personal data against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction, or damage.

stack.name: Cloud KMS (AWS KMS / Google Cloud KMS / Azure Key Vault)
stack.why: Managed, HSM-backed key management with envelope encryption and automatic key rotation — the default for encryption at rest of personal data in a cloud build.

stack.name: OpenBao (or HashiCorp Vault)
stack.why: Encryption-as-a-service: its transit engine does application-layer field encryption and reversible pseudonymization/tokenization without the app ever holding keys, plus dynamic secrets.

stack.name: cert-manager + Let's Encrypt
stack.why: Automates issuance and rotation of TLS certificates so all in-transit traffic is encrypted by default, with no manual cert lifecycle to forget.

stack.name: Linkerd (or Istio) service mesh
stack.why: Enforces automatic mutual-TLS between all internal services, giving confidentiality and integrity for east-west traffic that public TLS termination alone misses.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. OpenBao is the Linux Foundation open-source fork of Vault (relevant since Vault moved to the BSL license); pick Vault if you want the commercial/enterprise edition. For availability/resilience add provider-native encrypted backups + point-in-time recovery, which complement rather than replace the above.

capabilities.name: Instruction-bound access control & least privilege
capabilities.description: Authorization enforcement ensuring personnel and processors can only access and process personal data on documented instructions, backed by least-privilege access controls.

stack.name: OpenFGA
stack.why: Zanzibar-style relationship-based authorization (ReBAC) that models fine-grained, least-privilege access per resource, giving a queryable source of truth for who may touch which personal data.

stack.name: Open Policy Agent (OPA)
stack.why: Policy-as-code decision engine (Rego) that encodes documented processing instructions as versioned, auditable rules enforced uniformly across services and data pipelines.

stack.name: Keycloak
stack.why: Mature OIDC/SAML identity provider supplying authenticated subjects, RBAC/group scoping, and step-up controls that anchor the least-privilege model for personnel and processors.

stack.name: Amazon Verified Permissions (Cedar)
stack.why: Managed Cedar-based authorization service for teams wanting hosted, provably-analyzable fine-grained permissions instead of self-run policy infrastructure.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and actively maintained as of 2025-2026. Typical greenfield split: Keycloak for authN + coarse RBAC, then either OpenFGA (self-hosted ReBAC) or Verified Permissions/Cedar (managed) for fine-grained least-privilege authZ; OPA covers policy-as-code enforcement of documented processing instructions at service/gateway/CI layers. Choose OpenFGA vs. Amazon Verified Permissions based on self-host vs. managed preference — you generally would not run both.

capabilities.name: Backup, restore & availability resilience
capabilities.description: Backup and disaster-recovery capability that restores availability of and access to personal data in a timely manner after a physical or technical incident.

stack.name: AWS Backup
stack.why: Policy-driven, centralized backups across compute/DB/storage with cross-region and cross-account copy for tested DR, plus immutable Vault Lock for ransomware resilience.

stack.name: Velero
stack.why: De-facto Kubernetes-native backup/restore and cluster migration, snapshotting persistent volumes and cluster resources to object storage for timely workload recovery.

stack.name: pgBackRest
stack.why: Reliable PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery with incremental backups and WAL archiving, restoring personal data in the primary datastore to any moment after an incident.

stack.name: S3 (with versioning + Cross-Region Replication + Object Lock)
stack.why: Durable (11 nines), immutable, geo-replicated backup target that keeps restore artifacts available and tamper-proof after a physical or technical failure.

capabilities.stack_notes: Layered by tier: object storage is the immutable DR target; pgBackRest covers the relational datastore holding personal data; Velero covers containerized workloads; AWS Backup provides the org-wide policy/scheduling and cross-region orchestration. Substitute equivalents by cloud (Azure Backup / GCP Backup and DR; GCS or Azure Blob with versioning + object lock). All confirmed as widely adopted and actively maintained as of 2026; no web search needed.

capabilities.name: Security testing & effectiveness assessment
capabilities.description: A recurring process to test, assess, and evaluate the effectiveness of security measures protecting personal data (e.g. pen tests, control reviews, vulnerability scans).

stack.name: Trivy
stack.why: De-facto vulnerability scanner for containers, filesystems, IaC and dependencies — wire into CI to continuously scan for known CVEs and misconfigurations.

stack.name: OWASP ZAP
stack.why: Widely-adopted DAST tool for automated and manual web-app/API vulnerability testing, runnable in pipelines against staging environments.

stack.name: HackerOne (PTaaS / bug bounty)
stack.why: Delivers the recurring human pen-test and continuous crowdsourced testing that scanners can't, producing triaged findings and retest evidence for compliance.

stack.name: Vanta
stack.why: Continuous control monitoring across GDPR/SOC2/ISO27001 — automatically tests control effectiveness and collects the assessment evidence auditors require.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and well-supported as of 2025-2026. Alternatives if preferences differ: Nessus/Tenable or Wiz (managed) in place of Trivy for broader posture scanning; Burp Suite Pro (managed) instead of/alongside ZAP for DAST; Cobalt or Synack as PTaaS alternatives to HackerOne; Drata or Secureframe instead of Vanta for continuous control monitoring. The set spans the capability's three named activities: vulnerability scans (Trivy, ZAP), pen tests (HackerOne), and control reviews/effectiveness assessment (Vanta).

capabilities.name: Breach detection, register & notification
capabilities.description: Incident response pipeline that detects personal-data breaches, maintains an internal breach register, notifies the supervisory authority within 72 hours with required content and delay justification, propagates processor-to-controller alerts, and notifies affected subjects in plain language for high-risk breaches subject to defined exemptions.

stack.name: Wazuh
stack.why: SIEM/XDR platform that detects personal-data breaches via file-integrity, DLP-style rules, and log correlation, firing the alert that starts the pipeline.

stack.name: TheHive 5 (StrangeBee)
stack.why: Security incident-response platform providing the breach register (case DB) with SLA/72h timers, task templates, and an alert feed to ingest processor-to-controller notifications.

stack.name: OneTrust Incident & Breach Response
stack.why: Purpose-built GDPR module encoding 300+ breach laws: 72h supervisory-authority notification content, delay justification, risk assessment, exemption logic, and plain-language data-subject notices.

stack.name: n8n
stack.why: Workflow orchestrator that glues detection to register to notifications — propagating processor-to-controller alerts and dispatching subject/authority notifications with audit trails.

capabilities.stack_notes: Split recommended: open-source SIEM (Wazuh) + SIRP (TheHive) covers detection and case/register workflow with 72h SLA tracking; a dedicated GRC breach module (OneTrust, or TrustArc as alternative) is the pragmatic managed choice for jurisdiction-aware authority notification content, delay justification, exemption rules, and data-subject plain-language notices, which are hard to hand-roll compliantly. n8n handles cross-system propagation (processor->controller alerts, notification dispatch). Elastic Security is a viable managed/OSS alternative to Wazuh for detection. Sources: https://docs.strangebee.com/thehive/overview/ , https://www.onetrust.com/news/onetrust-enhances-incident-breach-response/ , https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/onetrust-updates-incident--breach-response-solution-to-automate-guidance-and-response-across-300-data-breach-laws-300853960.html

capabilities.name: DPIA & prior consultation workflow
capabilities.description: Data protection impact assessment process triggered for high-risk/enumerated processing, capturing required DPIA content, DPO consultation, optional data-subject input, periodic review on risk change, and prior consultation with the supervisory authority for unmitigated residual risk.

stack.name: OneTrust Assessment Automation (PIA/DPIA Automation)
stack.why: Market-leading privacy platform with purpose-built DPIA/PIA templates, risk scoring, DPO review routing, periodic re-assessment triggers, and supervisory-authority consultation tracking out of the box.

stack.name: CNIL PIA tool
stack.why: Free, regulator-authored (French DPA) DPIA methodology app that captures required Art. 35 content, structures risk analysis, and generates the assessment report — ideal as the assessment core in a self-hosted build.

stack.name: Camunda 8 (BPMN/DMN workflow engine)
stack.why: Orchestrates the DPIA lifecycle as a modeled process: high-risk-processing trigger, DPO consultation and optional data-subject input steps, periodic review on risk change, and escalation to prior consultation for unmitigated residual risk.

stack.name: Vanta
stack.why: Widely adopted GRC/compliance automation that ties DPIA outcomes into a continuous control and risk register, with review reminders and evidence trails linking privacy risk to SOC2/ISO27001 posture.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current as of 2025-2026. OneTrust is the dominant managed choice for a turnkey DPIA workflow; CNIL PIA + Camunda is the strong open-source pairing (assessment content + orchestration/prior-consultation escalation) for a self-hosted build; Vanta is an optional managed layer if DPIA must feed a broader continuous-compliance program. Alternatives worth noting: TrustArc / Osano (managed privacy platforms) and OpenPages/ServiceNow GRC for large-enterprise workflow orchestration.

capabilities.name: DPO designation & governance
capabilities.description: Designation of a qualified, independent Data Protection Officer with published contact details, adequate resources and access, protection from dismissal/conflicts, and assignment of statutory risk-based advisory and monitoring tasks.

stack.name: OneTrust Privacy & Data Governance Cloud
stack.why: Market-leading privacy management suite that hosts the RoPA, DPIA/assessment, and breach register a DPO statutorily monitors and advises on, with role-based access and audit trails that evidence independent oversight.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides
stack.why: Privacy-as-code data-mapping and DSAR platform that gives the DPO programmatic, continuous technical visibility into processing activities for monitoring rather than point-in-time spreadsheets.

stack.name: Osano
stack.why: Lighter-weight, widely-adopted privacy program + consent platform well-suited to a greenfield org, covering RoPA, vendor risk, and DPO reporting/dashboards for accountability.

stack.name: TrustArc Privacy Management Platform
stack.why: Established alternative privacy governance suite with built-in assessment workflows and DPO advisory/monitoring task tracking, useful where a validated regulatory content library is preferred.

capabilities.stack_notes: DPO designation is fundamentally an organizational/legal act (a qualified, independent person with published contact details and protected status) — no tool "implements" the role itself; published DPO contact details normally live in the site's privacy policy/DPA rather than a dedicated product. The components above are the privacy-governance platforms that operationalize the DPO's statutory risk-based advisory and monitoring tasks (RoPA, DPIA, breach register, DSAR, monitoring dashboards). Recommend picking one primary platform (OneTrust or Osano for most greenfield builds; Fides if a code-first/self-hosted, engineering-owned stack is preferred) rather than stacking several. All four confirmed active and widely adopted as of 2025-2026 from prior knowledge; not web-verified this session.

capabilities.name: Records of processing & authority cooperation
capabilities.description: Maintained records of processing activities (as controller and processor), designation of an EU representative for non-EU entities, and processes to cooperate with the supervisory authority on request.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides
stack.why: Privacy-as-code platform that auto-discovers data flows and generates/maintains Article 30 records of processing (RoPA) from your systems, versioned in the repo.

stack.name: OneTrust Data Mapping & RoPA (Privacy Automation)
stack.why: Market-leading privacy platform with a dedicated Article 30 RoPA module for controller/processor records plus regulator-interaction and DSAR workflows for authority cooperation.

stack.name: Prighter (GDPR/UK Representative-as-a-Service)
stack.why: Designated Article 27 EU (and UK) representative for non-EU entities, providing the listed EU contact point and handling correspondence with supervisory authorities on your behalf.

stack.name: Transcend
stack.why: Alternative privacy-ops platform that builds a live data inventory and continuously syncs it into RoPA/data-map records, reducing manual upkeep of processing activities.

capabilities.stack_notes: Core of this capability splits into three concerns: (1) maintaining RoPA as controller and processor — Fides (OSS) or OneTrust/Transcend (managed) keep the register current from actual data flows rather than static spreadsheets; (2) EU representative designation for non-EU entities — a distinct legal service, best met by a representative-as-a-service provider like Prighter (alternatives: DataRep, DataGuard); (3) supervisory-authority cooperation — handled via the representative plus the regulator-interaction/incident workflows in the privacy platform. For a lean greenfield build, Fides + Prighter covers OSS RoPA + Art. 27; swap in OneTrust or Transcend if you want a managed all-in-one with built-in DSAR and breach/authority workflows. Confidence is from prior knowledge (cutoff Jan 2026), not a fresh web check.

capabilities.name: Processor & joint-controller contracting
capabilities.description: Vendor governance that engages only processors giving sufficient guarantees, binds them with mandatory-clause written contracts, controls sub-processor authorization and flow-down liability, and formalizes joint-controller responsibility arrangements.

stack.name: OneTrust Third-Party Risk Management (with DPA/Vendorpedia)
stack.why: Runs processor due-diligence to evidence 'sufficient guarantees,' tracks sub-processors and authorization chains, and centralizes DPA records — the market-standard GRC choice for Art. 28 vendor governance.

stack.name: Vanta Vendor Risk Management
stack.why: Continuously collects and monitors each processor's security guarantees (SOC 2/ISO evidence, questionnaires) so engagement decisions and ongoing oversight are auditable in a modern build.

stack.name: Ironclad CLM
stack.why: Enforces mandatory-clause DPA templates and playbooks (flow-down liability, sub-processor authorization, joint-controller Art. 26 terms) with clause-level guardrails during contract negotiation and signature.

stack.name: Documenso
stack.why: Self-hostable e-signature platform to execute the required written processor and joint-controller contracts with tamper-evident audit trails, avoiding vendor lock-in for the signing step.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and actively maintained as of 2025-2026. Typical split: a TPRM/GRC platform (OneTrust or Vanta) for the 'sufficient guarantees' assessment + sub-processor tracking, a CLM (Ironclad) for mandatory-clause enforcement and flow-down/joint-controller terms, and a signing tool (Documenso, open-source; or DocuSign/Ironclad-native if fully managed) to formalize the written contracts. OneTrust and Vanta overlap on vendor assessment — pick one, not both. No mature open-source option covers the full TPRM/CLM workflow, so those tiers are managed by necessity.

capabilities.name: Cross-border transfer safeguards
capabilities.description: Controls governing personal-data transfers outside the EEA: enforcing Chapter V bases, relying on and monitoring adequacy decisions, applying appropriate safeguards (unmodified SCCs, BCRs, codes/certifications) with supplementary measures, rejecting foreign disclosure demands lacking an international legal basis, gating derogations to the specific situation with subject risk-warnings and last-resort documentation, and recording every derogation-based transfer.

stack.name: OneTrust (Data Mapping / Cross-Border Transfers module + Assessment Automation)
stack.why: Purpose-built register for Chapter V: maintains RoPA/transfer inventory keyed to each transfer basis (adequacy, SCCs, BCRs, Art.49 derogations), automates Transfer Impact Assessments with supplementary-measure tracking, and logs every derogation-based transfer for audit.

stack.name: Fides by Ethyca
stack.why: Code-native, self-hostable alternative that discovers and maps data flows across services and annotates them with destination/legal-basis metadata, so cross-border flows and their Chapter V basis are tracked in CI rather than a spreadsheet.

stack.name: AWS European Sovereign Cloud
stack.why: EU-operated, physically/logically isolated region (GA Jan 2026) that keeps personal data and operations inside the EEA, eliminating the transfer entirely for in-scope workloads and neutralizing foreign-disclosure exposure.

stack.name: HashiCorp Vault (with BYOK / external key management)
stack.why: Supplementary technical measure: holds encryption keys under EEA control so any data that does leave the region stays effectively unreadable, strengthening TIAs and supporting rejection of foreign disclosure demands that lack an international legal basis.

capabilities.stack_notes: Confirmed current via web search (July 2026): AWS European Sovereign Cloud reached GA on 2026-01-15 (independent EU-located region, Germany-first with expansion to BE/NL/PT); OneTrust's TIA/cross-border transfer tooling remains the market-standard for Chapter V documentation as of 2025-2026. Typical split: OneTrust or Fides for the governance/register/TIA + derogation-log layer (managed vs. open-source choice), plus residency (Sovereign Cloud, or Microsoft EU Data Boundary as an equivalent) and EEA-held keys (Vault) as the technical supplementary-measures layer. Adequacy-decision monitoring is a live-feed feature of OneTrust; an open-source stack would need a manual/scripted watch on the EU Commission adequacy list.

capabilities.name: Consent capture & lifecycle management
capabilities.description: A consent subsystem that records demonstrable proof of consent, presents consent requests distinctly in plain language separate from other terms, ensures consent is freely given (not a condition of service), lets subjects withdraw as easily as they gave it, and enforces the explicit-consent standard for special-category data.

stack.name: Didomi (Consent & Preference Management Platform)
stack.why: API-first CMP that records timestamped proof-of-consent, granular per-purpose choices, and a preference center for as-easy-as-given withdrawal; GDPR/IAB-TCF native and a 2026 enterprise leader (now Sourcepoint).

stack.name: OneTrust Consent & Preferences
stack.why: Most widely adopted enterprise consent platform, with immutable consent receipts, distinct plain-language consent notices, and explicit-consent handling for special-category data across web/app/backend.

stack.name: c15t
stack.why: Developer-first, self-hostable headless consent engine (React/Vue/Svelte/edge) giving full-code control over consent capture, an auditable consent-state store, and a built-in preference center for withdrawal.

stack.name: Usercentrics (incl. Cookiebot)
stack.why: Widely deployed EU-focused CMP with granular, freely-given consent flows, cross-domain consent logging/proof, and automated compliance updates across 150+ countries.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four target the same GDPR Art. 7/9 requirements (demonstrable proof, distinct plain-language requests, freely-given non-conditional consent, easy withdrawal, explicit consent for special-category data). For a new build, pick one CMP rather than stacking: Didomi or OneTrust if you want a managed record-of-consent API and enterprise governance; c15t if you want an open-source, self-hosted engine you embed and own end-to-end; Usercentrics/Cookiebot for a turnkey EU web deployment. Whichever you choose, persist consent receipts in your own datastore too so proof survives vendor changes. Sources: didomi.io/blog/enterprise-consent-management-platforms-best-cmp-2026, enzuzo.com/blog/best-consent-management-platforms, github.com/c15t/c15t, consent.io.

capabilities.name: Special-category & children's data protection
capabilities.description: Handling controls that block processing of special-category data unless an Article 9(2) exception applies, verify the child's age against the applicable threshold for online services offered to children, and make reasonable technology-based efforts to verify parental authorisation.

stack.name: Yoti (age assurance / facial age estimation)
stack.why: Regulator-approved facial age estimation + digital-ID age checks to verify a child's age against the applicable online-services threshold; yoti-003 ranked #1 by NIST for 13-16 age estimation.

stack.name: SuperAwesome Kids Web Services (KWS)
stack.why: Purpose-built verifiable-parental-consent toolkit (COPPA/GDPR-K) offering technology-based parent verification (payment card, ID scan, facial age estimation) — the most widely deployed VPC platform.

stack.name: OneTrust Consent & Preference Management
stack.why: Records and enforces explicit opt-in consent and lawful basis per purpose, so special-category (Art 9) processing is blocked unless a valid Art 9(2) exception/consent is on record.

stack.name: Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud DLP)
stack.why: Discovers and classifies special-category data (health, biometrics, race, etc.) in data flows and storage so pipelines can gate or de-identify it before processing.

capabilities.stack_notes: Coverage maps to the three sub-controls: age check (Yoti), parental authorisation (KWS), and special-category gating (OneTrust for consent/lawful-basis + Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection for detection/classification). Alternatives worth noting: Persona for age/identity verification, PRIVO for VPC (FTC safe harbor), Transcend or Osano for consent management, and AWS Macie / Microsoft Purview / BigID for sensitive-data discovery. Viable open-source substitutes are scarce for age assurance and VPC (these are inherently managed/regulated services); the closest OSS option is on the classification side (e.g. Microsoft Presidio for PII/special-category detection) if a self-hosted alternative to Google Cloud DLP is required.

capabilities.name: Data minimisation, accuracy & retention lifecycle
capabilities.description: Data-lifecycle machinery limiting collection to what is necessary, keeping data accurate and rectified/erased without delay, and enforcing defined retention periods with automated deletion or anonymisation of identifiable data when they expire.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides
stack.why: Privacy-as-code platform that maps PII and automates data-subject access/rectification/erasure plus per-dataset retention rules directly against your infrastructure.

stack.name: Transcend
stack.why: Developer-first DSR/erasure orchestration with APIs that propagate deletion and retention actions across microservices, SaaS, and data warehouses.

stack.name: pg_partman + pg_cron
stack.why: Time-based table partitioning with scheduled automatic dropping of expired partitions, giving deterministic retention/deletion at the Postgres storage layer.

stack.name: ARX Data Anonymization Tool
stack.why: Applies k-anonymity, pseudonymisation, and generalisation so identifiable data can be anonymised rather than deleted when retention periods expire.

capabilities.stack_notes: Split OSS-native (Fides for privacy-as-code, pg_partman/pg_cron for storage-level TTL, ARX for anonymisation-on-expiry) and managed (Transcend for cross-system DSR/erasure orchestration; OneTrust is the enterprise-suite alternative if a broader GRC platform is preferred over Transcend's developer/API focus). Fides + a storage-native TTL mechanism covers most greenfield builds; add ARX or Transcend when anonymisation-instead-of-delete or multi-system fan-out is required. Confirmed current for 2025-2026 via vendor sites and a 2026 privacy-platform buyer's guide.

capabilities.name: Data-subject transparency, complaints & remedies
capabilities.description: Subject-facing intake and information flows: clear plain-language notices at or before collection, informing subjects of and not obstructing their rights to lodge a supervisory-authority complaint and pursue an effective judicial remedy, accepting requests from mandated not-for-profit representatives, and a process to receive, track, and comply with binding supervisory-authority orders.

stack.name: Osano (Consent & CMP)
stack.why: Widely-adopted consent/CMP platform for serving clear plain-language privacy notices at or before collection and capturing consent records.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides
stack.why: Self-hostable privacy-engineering framework with a subject-facing request portal that receives, maps, and fulfills DSRs across connected systems.

stack.name: Transcend (DSR Automation)
stack.why: End-to-end privacy-request orchestration (1,500+ integrations) to authenticate, route, track, and fulfill requests — including those from mandated representatives — with an auditable workflow.

stack.name: Jira Service Management
stack.why: SLA-driven case/ticketing workflow to receive, track, and evidence compliance with binding supervisory-authority orders and complaint intake, with full audit trail.

capabilities.stack_notes: Currency confirmed via web search (July 2026): Ethyca Fides is actively maintained (Fides 2.x, GitHub ethyca/fides) and Transcend publishes a 2026 DSAR guide + live DSR Automation product. Design intent: Osano handles the transparency/notice-at-collection leg; Fides (OSS) or Transcend (managed) handle subject-facing intake + fulfillment and accepting not-for-profit representative requests; a case tracker (Jira Service Management, or the case module inside Transcend/OneTrust) covers receiving/tracking/complying with supervisory-authority orders and lodged complaints. The notice UX should also surface subjects' right to lodge a supervisory-authority complaint and pursue a judicial remedy (static content, no dedicated tool). OneTrust is a viable managed all-in-one alternative that spans notice + DSAR + case management if a single vendor is preferred over the Osano/Fides/Transcend split. Sources: https://github.com/ethyca/fides , https://www.ethyca.com/fides , https://transcend.io/platform/dsr-automation , https://transcend.io/blog/dsar

capabilities.name: Capacity planning & elastic scaling
capabilities.description: Continuously monitor compute, storage, and network utilization, forecast demand against available capacity, and provide manual or auto-scaling so the system meets demand before resources are exhausted and availability commitments are breached.

stack.name: Prometheus
stack.why: CNCF-standard time-series metrics engine that scrapes compute/storage/network utilization and is the data source scaling decisions and forecasts read from.

stack.name: KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling)
stack.why: Graduated CNCF project that scales workloads on real demand signals (queue depth, Prometheus metrics, HTTP RPS) well beyond basic HPA, scaling to and from zero.

stack.name: Karpenter
stack.why: Just-in-time node provisioner that adds/consolidates cluster capacity in seconds so compute is elastic before pods go unschedulable and SLAs breach.

stack.name: Grafana
stack.why: De-facto dashboarding and alerting layer over Prometheus for capacity trend visualization, forecasting panels, and threshold alerts ahead of exhaustion.

capabilities.stack_notes: Assumes a Kubernetes-based greenfield build, the dominant 2025-2026 substrate for elastic scaling. All four are current and widely adopted. Managed equivalents if not self-hosting: AWS Auto Scaling / EC2 Auto Scaling Groups + Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus + Amazon Managed Grafana, or GKE Autopilot with Cloud Monitoring; on cloud, Karpenter is native to EKS while GKE uses its built-in Cluster Autoscaler / node auto-provisioning. For statistical demand forecasting, Prometheus data can feed tools like Grafana ML or Facebook Prophet, but the four above cover the core continuous-monitor-plus-autoscale loop.

capabilities.name: Environmental safeguards & facility monitoring
capabilities.description: Protect hosting facilities against environmental hazards (fire, flood, power loss, temperature, humidity) and monitor environmental conditions with alerting so responders can act before an anomaly causes an outage.

stack.name: Cloud provider compliance attestations (AWS Artifact / Google Cloud Compliance Reports / Azure Service Trust Portal)
stack.why: For a cloud-hosted greenfield build, physical facility protections (fire suppression, flood, power, HVAC, temperature/humidity) are inherited from the provider and evidenced via their SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / ISO 27001 reports — the correct 'don't build it' answer for most 2026 stacks.

stack.name: Prometheus + Alertmanager with SNMP Exporter
stack.why: De-facto standard for ingesting environmental telemetry (temp, humidity, PDU power, UPS state via SNMP/IPMI) and firing threshold-based alerts before an anomaly becomes an outage.

stack.name: PagerDuty (or Opsgenie)
stack.why: On-call routing, escalation, and multi-channel notification so a human responder is actually paged and acknowledges when an environmental alert triggers.

stack.name: Sunbird DCIM (managed) or openDCIM (open-source)
stack.why: Only if you operate your own facility/colo: DCIM tracks rack-level environmental sensors, power chains, and thermal maps and centralizes hazard monitoring — skip entirely for pure-cloud deployments.

capabilities.stack_notes: Primary recommendation for most 2026 greenfield builds: host on a major cloud/colo and inherit environmental safeguards via the provider's attestations (component 1) — this capability is largely a shared-responsibility 'inherited control' rather than something you build. Components 2-3 cover the part you still own: monitoring your own equipment telemetry and alerting responders. Component 4 (DCIM) only applies if you run physical facility infrastructure yourself. All listed tools are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Business continuity & disaster recovery
capabilities.description: Maintain encrypted isolated backups and redundant failover infrastructure with defined RTO/RPO, document and periodically test BC/DR plans and backup restoration, and identify disruption risks with proportionate mitigation including risk-transfer such as insurance.

stack.name: restic
stack.why: Widely-adopted CLI backup tool giving client-side AES-256 encryption, deduplication, and append-only/immutable repositories to isolated object storage — the encrypted-isolated-backup primitive with fast, verifiable restores.

stack.name: AWS Backup with S3 Object Lock (cross-region/cross-account)
stack.why: Centralized, policy-driven backup with scheduled RPO windows, WORM immutability via Object Lock, and cross-region/cross-account copy for isolated ransomware-resistant DR copies and enforceable retention.

stack.name: Velero
stack.why: De-facto standard for Kubernetes backup/restore and cluster migration, enabling failover of workloads and persistent volumes to a redundant cluster/region to meet defined RTO.

stack.name: Terraform
stack.why: Codifies the redundant failover infrastructure as reproducible IaC so recovery environments can be rebuilt to a known-good state and BC/DR runbooks can be periodically test-executed against real infra.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026; no web search was needed. Together they cover encrypted isolated backups (restic, AWS Backup + Object Lock immutability), redundant failover with defined RTO/RPO (Velero, Terraform-provisioned multi-region infra), and testable restoration (all support restore/rebuild drills). The requirement's risk-transfer/insurance element (e.g., cyber insurance) is a procurement/governance control, not a software component, so it is intentionally not listed here. Managed alternatives worth noting per cloud: Azure Backup / Google Cloud Backup and DR; Veeam is a strong commercial cross-platform option if a single managed backup plane is preferred over restic.

capabilities.name: Data classification & confidentiality protection
capabilities.description: Establish criteria to identify and classify confidential information at creation/receipt, maintain an inventory of confidential assets and locations, label the data, and apply access controls and encryption throughout its retention period.

stack.name: Microsoft Purview Information Protection (sensitivity labels + DLP)
stack.why: Defines classification criteria and auto/manual sensitivity labels applied at creation/receipt, with policy-driven DLP that follows the label through the data's life.

stack.name: AWS Macie (or Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection / Cloud DLP)
stack.why: Continuously discovers, classifies, and inventories confidential data (PII, secrets) across object storage, giving the required asset-and-location inventory.

stack.name: HashiCorp Vault
stack.why: Central secrets/key management with transit encryption and dynamic keys, enforcing encryption of confidential data throughout its retention period.

stack.name: Open Policy Agent (OPA) with OpenFGA
stack.why: Policy-as-code and relationship-based authorization to enforce fine-grained, label-aware access controls on classified assets.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. Choice of Macie vs Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection should follow the target cloud; both are managed discovery/classification services. Purview is the strongest labeling layer if the org is on Microsoft 365/Azure; a cloud-native alternative is AWS/GCP tag-based classification plus their DLP service. Vault vs cloud KMS (AWS KMS / Cloud KMS) is an open-source-vs-managed tradeoff for the encryption/key layer.

capabilities.name: Data retention & secure disposal
capabilities.description: Define retention periods aligned to commitments and legal obligations, then irreversibly delete or anonymize data at end-of-life (cryptographic erasure, secure wipe, physical destruction) across all copies including backups, retaining evidence of disposal.

stack.name: HashiCorp Vault
stack.why: Per-tenant/per-record encryption keys enable cryptographic erasure (crypto-shredding) — destroying the key renders data irrecoverable across all copies including backups.

stack.name: AWS S3 Object Lock + Lifecycle policies
stack.why: Declarative retention periods (governance/compliance mode) with automatic expiration and deletion of objects at end-of-life, tamper-evident and auditable.

stack.name: OpenMetadata
stack.why: Data catalog + governance to classify PII and define/track retention periods per dataset aligned to legal and contractual obligations.

stack.name: ShredOS / nwipe
stack.why: Standards-based secure wipe of physical media (NIST 800-88 style) producing a certificate as evidence of disposal for decommissioned drives.

capabilities.stack_notes: Recommended pattern for a greenfield build: make cryptographic erasure the primary disposal mechanism (Vault-managed keys) since it uniformly covers backups and replicas that secure-wipe cannot reach; use S3 Object Lock/Lifecycle for automated retention+expiry of object data; OpenMetadata to author and enforce retention schedules; ShredOS/nwipe only for the residual physical-media destruction case. Disposal evidence: retain KMS key-destruction logs (CloudTrail/Vault audit device) and wipe certificates as the immutable audit trail. Cloud-neutral alternatives exist (GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, MinIO object retention) if avoiding AWS lock-in.

capabilities.name: Control environment: governance, ethics & personnel
capabilities.description: Maintain a code of conduct with ethics remediation, an independent competent board overseeing controls, defined organizational structure and authorities with segregation of duties, plus role-based competence requirements, training, succession, and individual accountability for control responsibilities.

stack.name: NAVEX One (Ethics & Compliance suite)
stack.why: Purpose-built for code of conduct policy management, ethics hotline intake, and case/remediation workflows — the core of ethics-remediation and individual accountability.

stack.name: Vanta (or Drata) GRC platform
stack.why: Maps controls to owners with evidence and continuous monitoring, operationalizing board-overseen control responsibility and per-role accountability across SOC 2/ISO 27001.

stack.name: Rippling (or Workday) HRIS
stack.why: Encodes the org structure, reporting lines, role-based competence/job profiles, training assignments, and succession data that define authorities and personnel controls.

stack.name: SailPoint Identity Security (or open-source Keycloak for RBAC)
stack.why: Enforces segregation of duties and least-privilege authorities via identity governance, access reviews, and SoD-conflict detection tied to defined roles.

capabilities.stack_notes: Domain is governance/HR/ethics-heavy, so strong options are predominantly managed SaaS; the credible open-source foothold is Keycloak for role-based authorities (RBAC), noted as the alternative in the identity component. Vanta/Drata and Rippling/Workday and SailPoint/Keycloak are given as interchangeable peers so the build can pick by budget/scale. All named tools are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Control information & communications
capabilities.description: Identify and capture quality information needed for internal control from internal and external sources, and communicate control objectives, policies, and responsibilities internally (including a confidential reporting channel), to the board, and to external users.

stack.name: Vanta (or Drata)
stack.why: GRC platform that captures control information from integrated internal/external systems and centralizes control objectives, policies, ownership, and attestations — its Trust Center also communicates control posture to external users.

stack.name: GlobaLeaks
stack.why: Anonymous, end-to-end-encrypted whistleblowing platform (EU Directive 2019/1937 / ISO 37002 aligned) that provides the required confidential internal reporting channel; self-hostable with no per-seat cost.

stack.name: Confluence (or Notion)
stack.why: Internal knowledge hub for publishing and versioning control objectives, policies, and role/responsibility assignments so they are consistently communicated to staff, with permissioned spaces for external stakeholders.

stack.name: Diligent Boards
stack.why: Secure board portal for communicating control objectives, risks, and governance responsibilities to the board with auditable distribution and acknowledgement.

capabilities.stack_notes: Maps to COSO principles 13-15 (uses quality information; communicates internally; communicates externally). Split: Vanta = capture/aggregate control information + external users; GlobaLeaks = confidential reporting channel; Confluence/Notion = internal policy communication; Diligent = board communication. Vanta and Drata are both current 2025-2026 market leaders (Vanta named IDC MarketScape Leader 2025); GlobaLeaks confirmed actively maintained and recommended by Transparency International. A leaner 3-component build can fold board comms into the Confluence/Notion hub; Diligent is warranted mainly when a formal board portal with acknowledgement tracking is required. NAVEX EthicsPoint is the managed alternative to GlobaLeaks if a fully hosted hotline (with phone intake) is preferred.

capabilities.name: Identity & access management
capabilities.description: Logical access layer that assigns unique identifiers, manages credential issuance/rotation/revocation, enforces MFA on privileged/remote/external paths, runs authorized provisioning and prompt deprovisioning, applies least privilege and segregation of duties, and performs recurring access and privileged-access recertification.

stack.name: Microsoft Entra ID + Entra ID Governance
stack.why: Cloud IdP giving each user a unique ID with Conditional Access MFA on privileged/remote/external paths, plus PIM for just-in-time privileged access and Access Reviews/lifecycle workflows for provisioning, deprovisioning, and recurring recertification.

stack.name: Okta Workforce Identity Cloud
stack.why: Widely-adopted IdP with adaptive/phishing-resistant MFA and SCIM-based lifecycle provisioning that automates authorized joiner-mover-leaver credential issuance, rotation, and prompt revocation across downstream apps.

stack.name: SailPoint Identity Security Cloud
stack.why: Leading IGA layer that enforces least privilege and segregation-of-duties policies and runs the scheduled access and privileged-access certification campaigns the capability requires.

stack.name: Keycloak
stack.why: Self-hostable OIDC/SAML identity provider for your own app's login layer, issuing unique identities and enforcing MFA/credential policies without vendor lock-in.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and actively maintained as of 2025-2026. Entra ID Governance and SailPoint specifically cover the SoD/least-privilege/recertification governance controls; Entra/Okta/Keycloak cover the authentication, MFA, and credential-lifecycle controls. A typical greenfield build pairs one IdP (Entra, Okta, or Keycloak) with an IGA tool (Entra ID Governance or SailPoint) rather than adopting all four.

capabilities.name: Encryption & cryptographic key management
capabilities.description: Protect sensitive and personal data with encryption at rest and in transit, restrict how and where such data may be transmitted, and securely manage cryptographic keys across their full lifecycle (generation, storage, rotation, destruction).

stack.name: Cloud provider KMS (AWS KMS / Google Cloud KMS / Azure Key Vault)
stack.why: HSM-backed managed key lifecycle (generation, rotation, destruction, access policy) with envelope encryption that underpins at-rest encryption for the rest of the stack.

stack.name: HashiCorp Vault (or OpenBao, its OSS/Linux Foundation fork)
stack.why: Central secrets + encryption-as-a-service: the Transit engine encrypts app data without exposing keys, with dynamic secrets, automated key rotation, and audit logging you can self-host.

stack.name: cert-manager + Let's Encrypt
stack.why: Automates TLS certificate issuance and renewal in Kubernetes so encryption-in-transit (HTTPS/mTLS) stays valid without manual cert rotation.

stack.name: Google Tink
stack.why: Misuse-resistant application-layer crypto library that gives safe AEAD/envelope-encryption primitives and integrates with cloud KMS for key wrapping, avoiding hand-rolled crypto mistakes.

capabilities.stack_notes: Typical 2026 greenfield pattern: a cloud KMS (or Vault/OpenBao Transit) is the root of trust for key lifecycle and envelope/at-rest encryption; TLS everywhere (cert-manager + Let's Encrypt, optionally a service mesh like Istio/Linkerd for mTLS) covers in-transit; Tink handles field/application-level encryption safely. Vault/OpenBao and a cloud KMS are somewhat alternatives — pick cloud KMS if fully managed is preferred, Vault/OpenBao if you need self-hosted, multi-cloud, or richer secrets management. Data-residency/transmission restrictions are enforced via KMS key-region policies + IAM/network egress controls rather than a distinct tool.

capabilities.name: Control monitoring, evaluation & deficiency remediation
capabilities.description: Run ongoing monitoring and periodic independent evaluations against a documented control baseline, document and retain results, then assess and rank identified deficiencies, communicate them, track corrective actions to completion, and escalate significant deficiencies to senior management/board.

stack.name: Vanta
stack.why: Continuous control monitoring against a documented framework baseline (SOC2/ISO27001/GDPR): auto-collects evidence, flags failing controls as deficiencies, and retains audit-ready results.

stack.name: Prowler
stack.why: Independent, automated technical evaluation of cloud controls against baselines (CIS, SOC2, ISO, GDPR) — schedule periodic scans that objectively test the control set separate from the GRC tool.

stack.name: Grafana + Prometheus/Loki (Grafana Labs LGTM stack)
stack.why: The ongoing logging & monitoring backbone — alerting on control-signal drift plus dashboards that surface ranked deficiency status for senior-management/board reporting.

stack.name: Jira Service Management
stack.why: Tracks assessed and ranked deficiencies as corrective-action items to completion, with SLA/escalation rules to route significant deficiencies to leadership.

capabilities.stack_notes: Vanta is interchangeable with Drata (both widely adopted managed CCM platforms); pick one. Prowler is the most widely adopted OSS control-evaluation scanner (Steampipe/Powerpipe compliance benchmarks are an alternative). Pattern: managed CCM for baseline+evidence+deficiency detection, OSS scanner for independent testing, observability stack for continuous monitoring/board dashboards, and an issue tracker for corrective-action-to-completion with escalation. All confirmed current for 2025-2026 from domain knowledge (cutoff Jan 2026); no web search performed.

capabilities.name: External communication & incident reporting channels
capabilities.description: Provide channels for external parties to report security incidents, vulnerabilities, and complaints, notify external users of changes affecting security commitments, and select communication methods, formats, and timing appropriate to audience and urgency.

stack.name: HackerOne
stack.why: Industry-standard VDP + bug bounty platform giving external researchers a structured, triaged channel to report security vulnerabilities.

stack.name: security.txt (RFC 9116)
stack.why: Standardized /.well-known/security.txt file publishes a machine-readable security contact so external parties know exactly where and how to report incidents.

stack.name: Atlassian Statuspage
stack.why: Proactively notifies subscribed external users of incidents and changes affecting security commitments via email/SMS/webhook with severity-appropriate messaging.

stack.name: Zammad
stack.why: Self-hosted help-desk providing an auditable intake channel for external complaints and reports across email, web form, and chat.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted in 2025-2026. HackerOne (or Bugcrowd as an equivalent managed alternative) covers vulnerability intake; security.txt is the open standard advertising the reporting contact; Statuspage (or open-source Cachet / managed Instatus) handles outbound change/incident notification tuned to audience and urgency; Zammad (or managed Zendesk/Freshdesk) captures complaints. Together they cover inbound reporting, contact discoverability, and outbound notification called for by the capability.

capabilities.name: Risk assessment & fraud-risk governance
capabilities.description: Specify objectives and risk tolerances, identify and analyze risks to objectives from internal and external sources, determine documented risk responses, explicitly assess fraud potential including management override, and re-analyze risk when significant environmental, business, leadership, or technology changes occur.

stack.name: LogicGate Risk Cloud
stack.why: No-code GRC/ERM platform with configurable risk register, risk tolerances, and workflow-driven risk responses plus automated re-assessment triggers on change events.

stack.name: Diligent HighBond (Diligent One)
stack.why: 2025 Gartner GRC Leader whose ML-driven analytics test fraud potential and management-override / journal-entry anomalies while managing enterprise risk assessments.

stack.name: Eramba
stack.why: Self-hostable GRC tool providing an internal/external risk register, documented risk treatment, and scheduled periodic reviews to re-analyze risk on significant change.

stack.name: SimpleRisk
stack.why: Lightweight open-source risk assessment/register with scoring, documented mitigation responses, and configurable review cycles for greenfield teams wanting minimal footprint.

capabilities.stack_notes: Capability maps to COSO ERM principles 6-9 (objectives/tolerances, risk identification, fraud assessment incl. management override, change-driven re-analysis). Managed picks (LogicGate, Diligent HighBond) are the widely-adopted enterprise choices; Diligent HighBond is the strongest for the fraud-potential/management-override requirement via its analytics engine. Open-source picks (Eramba, SimpleRisk) cover the risk-register + treatment + periodic-review core but need custom analytics for fraud-specific override testing. Both managed tools confirmed current for 2025-2026 via web search (LogicGate won a Oct-2025 risk award; Diligent named 2025 Gartner GRC Magic Quadrant Leader). Choose 1 managed platform + optionally 1 open-source register depending on budget/self-hosting needs.

capabilities.name: Control framework design, policy deployment & accountability
capabilities.description: Select and develop a risk-aligned mix of manual/automated and preventive/detective control activities, deploy them through documented policies and procedures with assigned accountability, perform them timely with corrective action, and periodically reassess them via competent personnel.

stack.name: Vanta
stack.why: Widely-adopted compliance automation platform that maps a risk-aligned control set to frameworks (SOC 2/ISO 27001/GDPR), ships policy templates, and runs continuous automated (detective) checks with evidence collection.

stack.name: Drata
stack.why: GRC platform whose strength is control ownership and accountability — assign each control to a person, drive timely completion and corrective-action workflows, and schedule periodic control reassessment.

stack.name: Eramba
stack.why: Self-hostable GRC for teams needing full control: design a custom control catalog, run the policy lifecycle (review/approval/publish), assign owners, and enforce periodic reassessment on defined review cycles.

stack.name: NIST OSCAL + IBM trestle
stack.why: Open standard and toolkit for expressing controls, policies, and assessment results as machine-readable, version-controlled 'compliance-as-code', so the framework lives in your repo and stays auditable across tools.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current as of 2025-2026. Vanta and Drata are the two dominant managed options — pick one, not both; Vanta leans toward framework breadth and automated evidence, Drata toward control accountability and corrective-action workflows. Eramba is the leading open-source self-hosted alternative when data residency or customization rules out a SaaS. OSCAL/trestle is complementary (not a full platform): adopt it if you want controls and policies as code alongside whichever platform you choose. Secureframe and Sprinto are viable managed alternatives in the same tier if evaluating further. Confidence is high from domain knowledge; no web search was needed.

capabilities.name: Vendor & third-party risk management
capabilities.description: Maintain a vendor/subprocessor inventory, assess risk at onboarding and ongoing, impose security/confidentiality/availability and retention/disposal obligations contractually, monitor subservice-organization controls, remediate deficiencies, and manage secure termination including data return/destruction and access revocation.

stack.name: Vanta (Vendor Risk Management module)
stack.why: Auto-discovers and maintains a vendor/subprocessor inventory, runs onboarding + recurring risk assessments, and automates security questionnaires/document collection with continuous monitoring.

stack.name: SecurityScorecard
stack.why: Continuous external security ratings and alerting on vendors and subservice organizations, surfacing control deficiencies to drive ongoing monitoring and remediation.

stack.name: OneTrust Third-Party Risk Management
stack.why: Enterprise VRM workflows for assessment, contractual obligation/DPA tracking (security, confidentiality, retention/disposal), and structured offboarding covering data return/destruction and access revocation.

stack.name: Eramba (Community Edition)
stack.why: Self-hostable GRC with a third-party register, recurring risk assessments, and control/obligation tracking for teams that need on-prem TPRM instead of SaaS.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and actively supported as of 2025-2026. Typical greenfield pattern: one automation/GRC platform of record (Vanta for mid-market, OneTrust for enterprise-depth contractual/offboarding obligations, or Eramba if self-hosting is required) plus a continuous external-monitoring feed like SecurityScorecard (BitSight is an equivalent alternative). Drata is a close substitute for Vanta; Prevalent/Mitratech and ServiceNow VRM are enterprise alternatives to OneTrust. Contract lifecycle (CLM) tools like Ironclad may complement the contractual-obligation piece if not handled inside the GRC platform. Did not web-verify each vendor live this session; all are well-established and were current at knowledge cutoff.

capabilities.name: Physical access control & secure media disposal
capabilities.description: Restrict and periodically review physical access to facilities, data centers, and hardware, and securely erase or destroy data on media and assets before disposal or reuse so residual sensitive data is unrecoverable.

stack.name: Cloud provider (AWS / Azure / GCP) inherited data-center controls
stack.why: Building on a hyperscaler inherits SOC2/ISO27001-attested data-center physical access control and NIST 800-88 media destruction, so you never operate or dispose of your own server media.

stack.name: Verkada or Kisi cloud access control
stack.why: Cloud-managed badge/door access for your own offices and hardware rooms, with tamper-evident audit logs that make the required periodic access reviews auditable.

stack.name: Kandji / Jamf / Microsoft Intune (MDM)
stack.why: Enforces FileVault/BitLocker full-disk encryption plus remote wipe, so device disposal or reuse becomes a verifiable crypto-erase that renders residual data unrecoverable.

stack.name: Vanta or Drata (GRC automation)
stack.why: Automates the periodic physical-access review workflow and centrally collects device-disposal/destruction evidence and vendor SOC2 reports for continuous audit readiness.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are managed/SaaS because this capability is fundamentally about facilities, hardware, and endpoints rather than application code — there is no meaningful open-source "component" you embed in a software stack to control physical door access or destroy data-center drives. For self-managed endpoints/servers, an open-source disk sanitizer such as nwipe (NIST 800-88 purge) or the built-in `cryptsetup`/`blkdiscard` crypto-erase can supplement the MDM path, but in a greenfield cloud build the provider handles media destruction.
