Primary control set is: inherit DC controls from the cloud provider, gate your own facilities with cloud access control, enforce encryption+remote-wipe via MDM for crypto-shredding, and track reviews/evidence in a GRC platform.

capabilities.name: Infrastructure, network boundary & endpoint protection
capabilities.description: General controls over technology infrastructure (networks, servers, cloud) supporting reliable processing, boundary defenses (firewalls, segmentation, IDS/IPS) protecting the perimeter, and controls to prevent, detect, and remediate unauthorized or malicious software.

stack.name: Cloudflare (WAF + DDoS + Zero Trust/Access)
stack.why: Managed perimeter defense — global WAF, L3/7 DDoS mitigation, and identity-aware Zero Trust access replace legacy edge firewalls for a cloud-native build.

stack.name: Cilium + Hubble (eBPF)
stack.why: CNCF-graduated eBPF dataplane enforcing default-deny network policies and east-west microsegmentation for Kubernetes, with Hubble for flow visibility.

stack.name: CrowdStrike Falcon
stack.why: Widely-adopted EDR/XDR for servers, endpoints, and cloud workloads — prevents, detects, and remediates malicious software with cloud-delivered threat intel.

stack.name: Falco
stack.why: CNCF runtime threat detection using eBPF/syscalls to flag unexpected process, file, and network behavior in containers and hosts as an IDS layer.

capabilities.stack_notes: Scoped to a greenfield cloud/Kubernetes stack. Cloudflare handles the perimeter (boundary defense), Cilium handles internal segmentation, and Falcon+Falco cover endpoint/workload anti-malware and runtime intrusion detection. Open-source-only alternative to Falcon: Wazuh (HIDS, anti-malware, file-integrity monitoring). If not on Kubernetes, substitute cloud-provider network firewalls (e.g. AWS Network Firewall) for Cilium.

capabilities.name: Vulnerability management & remediation
capabilities.description: Scheduled scanning of infrastructure and software for known vulnerabilities and configuration drift, with tracked, risk-prioritized remediation to resolution within defined SLAs.

stack.name: Trivy
stack.why: Single scanner covering OS packages, language dependencies, container images, and IaC/config misconfiguration (drift), runnable on a schedule in CI or as a Kubernetes operator.

stack.name: Wiz
stack.why: Agentless CNAPP that continuously scans the cloud estate and contextually risk-prioritizes findings by exploitability, exposure, and blast radius rather than raw CVSS.

stack.name: DefectDojo
stack.why: Central vulnerability aggregation/deduplication hub that ingests all scanner outputs and tracks risk-based remediation against configurable SLAs with reporting.

stack.name: Snyk
stack.why: Developer-facing SCA/SAST/container scanning that opens automated fix pull requests, driving software-side remediation to resolution inside the dev workflow.

capabilities.stack_notes: Pattern: Trivy (self-hosted scanning) or Wiz (managed cloud scanning + prioritization) feed findings into DefectDojo, which enforces SLA tracking and remediation workflow; Snyk covers the software/dependency side with auto-fix PRs. Managed alternatives to Wiz in this space include Tenable, Qualys VMDR, and Orca Security. A lighter open-source software-side alternative to Snyk is OSV-Scanner plus Dependabot/Renovate. All four listed tools are current and widely adopted as of 2026; no web search was needed given their established market position.

capabilities.name: System monitoring, alerting & audit log retention
capabilities.description: Continuously monitor system components for anomalies with detection tooling and defined alerting thresholds that generate timely actionable alerts, and retain integrity-protected security logs supporting detection and post-hoc investigation.

stack.name: Prometheus + Alertmanager
stack.why: De-facto metrics monitoring stack: scrapes system/app metrics, encodes anomaly-detection rules with defined thresholds, and Alertmanager routes deduplicated, actionable alerts to PagerDuty/Slack/email.

stack.name: Grafana Loki + Grafana
stack.why: Horizontally-scalable log aggregation with unified dashboards and log-based alerting, giving one pane of glass over metrics and security logs for detection and post-hoc investigation.

stack.name: Wazuh
stack.why: Widely-used open SIEM/XDR that does continuous anomaly and intrusion detection, file-integrity monitoring, and correlation of security events for both real-time alerting and forensic audit review.

stack.name: AWS S3 with Object Lock (WORM)
stack.why: Immutable, integrity-protected long-term retention of security/audit logs via write-once-read-many Object Lock and configurable retention periods, satisfying tamper-evident audit-trail requirements.

capabilities.stack_notes: Pattern: Prometheus/Alertmanager for metric-threshold alerting, Loki/Grafana for log analytics and dashboards, Wazuh for security detection and file-integrity monitoring, and S3 Object Lock as the immutable retention tier. Fully-managed alternative if avoiding self-hosting: Datadog (Infrastructure Monitoring + Cloud SIEM + Log Management with retention/archival to immutable storage) or Grafana Cloud, either of which collapses components 1-3 into one SaaS. On GCP/Azure the immutable-retention equivalent is GCS Bucket Lock or Azure Blob immutable storage. All listed tools are actively maintained and current as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Incident response & recovery
capabilities.description: End-to-end incident lifecycle covering triage and severity evaluation, a documented and periodically tested IR plan, containment/eradication/mitigation, breach and stakeholder communication, recovery of affected systems, and post-incident root-cause review with corrective actions.

stack.name: PagerDuty
stack.why: Industry-standard on-call scheduling, alert routing, and severity-based escalation — the triage/detection entry point that pages the right responders and starts the incident clock.

stack.name: incident.io
stack.why: Slack/Teams-native end-to-end incident lifecycle: declare, assign roles, track severity/timeline, drive stakeholder comms, and run structured post-incident (RCA) reviews with tracked follow-up actions.

stack.name: Cachet
stack.why: Self-hosted public/stakeholder status page for breach and outage communication, giving a supported OSS alternative to Atlassian Statuspage for external incident updates.

capabilities.stack_notes: Distinct-layer split rather than overlapping platforms: PagerDuty = detection/triage/on-call, incident.io = lifecycle orchestration + comms + post-incident RCA (covers the "documented, periodically tested IR plan" via runbooks and post-mortem workflows), Cachet = external stakeholder communication. Deliberately avoided two now-declining tools: Atlassian Opsgenie (end-of-sale June 2025, full EOL April 2027) and Grafana OnCall OSS (maintenance mode, archived 2026-03-24). Managed alternatives to incident.io in the same tier: Rootly and FireHydrant, both widely adopted in 2025-2026. If a managed status page is acceptable, Atlassian Statuspage is the market default in place of Cachet. Recovery of affected systems (DR/restore) is typically handled by the underlying infra/backup stack rather than these IR tools.

capabilities.name: Change management & secure SDLC
capabilities.description: Formal change process governing authorization, design/impact assessment, testing, independent approval, and implementation, with segregation of duties, version control, separated dev/test/prod environments, baseline configuration and security review, emergency-change and rollback paths, plus general controls over software acquisition, development, and maintenance and their technology dependencies.

stack.name: GitHub (branch protection + CODEOWNERS + required reviews)
stack.why: PR-based change flow enforces authorization, independent approval, and segregation of duties on top of git version control.

stack.name: GitHub Actions with Environments + required reviewers
stack.why: Gated CI/CD pipeline runs tests and enforces manual approval before promoting through separated dev/test/prod environments.

stack.name: OpenTofu (Terraform-compatible IaC)
stack.why: Versioned, reviewable baseline configuration for infrastructure with plan/apply gates and drift detection.

stack.name: Argo CD (GitOps)
stack.why: Declarative Git-driven deploys to prod with one-click/auto rollback to any prior known-good revision, supporting emergency-change paths.

capabilities.stack_notes: Set chosen for a greenfield 2026 build; all are widely adopted and current as of 2025-2026. GitHub + Actions cover the formal change process (authorization, independent approval, SoD via CODEOWNERS, testing gates, environment separation). OpenTofu covers baseline configuration-as-code; add a pipeline security scanner such as Trivy or Snyk for the security-review step if a 5th slot is available. Argo CD provides the implementation + rollback path. GitLab (managed or self-hosted) is a viable single-vendor alternative covering the first three roles.

capabilities.name: Privacy notice, consent & lawful collection
capabilities.description: Publish a privacy notice describing collection, use, retention, disclosure, and disposal of personal information at or before collection, and operate a consent ledger and collection controls that capture affirmative/explicit consent, verify source authority, and keep collection and use within notified purposes.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides
stack.why: Privacy-as-code platform that serves privacy notices, records consent against a shared data-use/purpose ontology, and enforces purpose limitation in the runtime — a self-hostable spine for the whole capability.

stack.name: OneTrust Consent & Preference Management
stack.why: Widely-adopted enterprise CMP for publishing/versioning privacy notices and capturing granular affirmative consent with a full audit trail at or before collection.

stack.name: Ketch (Progressive Consent / Data Permissioning)
stack.why: Server-side consent ledger that propagates purpose-based permissions across CDPs, ad, and AI pipelines in real time, keeping downstream use inside the notified purposes.

stack.name: Klaro!
stack.why: Lightweight, self-hosted web consent manager for explicit opt-in capture at the point of collection when you only need first-party notice + affirmative consent on the client.

capabilities.stack_notes: Fides is the recommended open-source foundation (notice + consent ledger + purpose enforcement, GDPR/CCPA/LGPD built in). OneTrust or Ketch are the mature managed alternatives — Ketch is notable for a server-side ledger that enforces purpose limitation across the data ecosystem. Klaro covers only the front-end capture slice and pairs with a backend ledger. Source authority verification (proving a valid collection source/legal basis) is typically handled by the ledger's consent-record metadata plus your own IAM/identity layer; no single tool fully covers it. Confirmed current 2025-2026: ethyca/fides (github.com/ethyca/fides), ketch.com (Progressive Consent launched 2025).

capabilities.name: Data-subject rights & complaint handling
capabilities.description: Authenticated self-service and back-office workflows that let data subjects access, correct, amend, or delete their personal information and propagate changes to third parties, plus an intake-and-resolution process for privacy inquiries, complaints, and disputes with corrective-action tracking.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides (with Lethe DSR engine)
stack.why: Open-source privacy-engineering platform that data-maps personal data across systems and executes access/rectify/erase DSR fulfillment as code, including downstream/third-party propagation.

stack.name: Transcend
stack.why: Managed data-subject-request automation that discovers and actions a requestor's data across all connected systems and third parties, with a hosted self-service intake portal.

stack.name: OneTrust Privacy & Data Governance (DSR Automation + Privacy Incident/Complaint Management)
stack.why: Widely-adopted suite pairing DSAR automation with privacy inquiry/complaint intake, dispute triage, and corrective-action tracking in one back-office workflow.

stack.name: OpenGDPR / self-hosted case management (e.g. Zammad or Camunda) fronting the DSR engine
stack.why: Open-source ticketing/BPMN workflow to run authenticated intake, resolution SLAs, and corrective-action tracking for complaints when a managed privacy suite is not desired.

capabilities.stack_notes: Verified current for 2025-2026 via web search. Typical build: Fides or Transcend for the automated DSR access/correct/delete + third-party propagation layer, plus OneTrust (managed) or an open-source case/BPMN tool (Zammad/Camunda) for complaint intake, disputes, and corrective-action tracking. OneTrust and Transcend are the most widely-adopted managed options; Ethyca Fides is the leading open-source DSR-automation engine. Sources: https://www.ethyca.com/guides/dsar-personal-data-tracking-infrastructure , https://www.onetrust.com/products/data-subject-request-dsr-automation/ , https://www.g2.com/compare/onetrust-privacy-automation-vs-transcend

capabilities.name: Privacy breach detection & notification
capabilities.description: Process and tooling to identify, track, and report unauthorized use or disclosure of personal information, notifying affected data subjects and regulators within required timeframes.

stack.name: Wazuh
stack.why: SIEM/XDR that detects unauthorized access and exfiltration of personal data via log analysis, file-integrity monitoring, and threat-detection rules — the breach-detection trigger.

stack.name: TheHive (StrangeBee)
stack.why: Incident-response case management to track each suspected breach, coordinate investigation, and keep a defensible audit timeline of who did what when.

stack.name: OneTrust Incident & Breach Response
stack.why: Assesses each incident against GDPR/CCPA/state-law obligations and drives data-subject and regulator notifications within statutory deadlines (e.g. GDPR 72h).

stack.name: Microsoft Purview (DSPM / data classification)
stack.why: Discovers and classifies where personal data lives and flags anomalous access, so a breach's scope — which subjects and record types are affected — is known quickly.

capabilities.stack_notes: Split by function: Wazuh = detection signal, TheHive = investigation/tracking, OneTrust = the statutory notification workflow (the part most specific to this capability), Purview/DSPM = knowing what personal data was exposed to scope notifications. All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. Alternatives worth noting: Cyera or BigID in place of Purview for DSPM; Vanta/Drata incident modules as a lighter managed alternative to OneTrust for smaller builds; TheHive can be swapped for a general SOAR if one is already in the stack. A minimal 2-tool build could be Wazuh + OneTrust.

capabilities.name: Personal data quality management
capabilities.description: Mechanisms that keep stored personal information accurate, complete, and relevant to the purposes for which it is used.

stack.name: Great Expectations
stack.why: Declarative expectation suites validate personal records for accuracy, completeness, and format at pipeline boundaries, with data docs for auditable proof.

stack.name: Soda Core (SodaCL)
stack.why: SQL-based data quality checks (missing/duplicate/stale rows, freshness, distribution) run in CI and on schedule to keep stored personal data correct and current.

stack.name: dbt (tests + snapshots)
stack.why: Built-in and generic tests enforce not-null/unique/accepted-values on PII columns while snapshots track change history so data stays relevant to its purpose.

stack.name: Monte Carlo
stack.why: End-to-end data observability with automated anomaly/freshness/volume monitoring and lineage, catching personal-data quality drift across warehouses at scale.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. Open-source options (Great Expectations, Soda Core, dbt) cover in-pipeline validation and are typically layered together; Monte Carlo (or alternatives like Ataccama ONE / Collibra DQ for MDM-heavy needs) adds managed observability. A pragmatic new build usually pairs dbt tests + Soda/Great Expectations for enforcement, adding a managed observability layer only when data estate grows.

capabilities.name: Processing integrity: validation, pipeline & output verification
capabilities.description: Documented processing specifications with intake controls validating inputs and authorizing sources, exactly-once complete/accurate/timely pipeline execution with dead-letter and reconciliation, and pre-release output verification, authorized delivery, and durable protected storage of inputs and outputs.

stack.name: Temporal
stack.why: Durable execution engine gives exactly-once, idempotent pipeline steps with automatic retries, timeouts, and built-in dead-letter/compensation — the backbone for complete/accurate/timely processing.

stack.name: Great Expectations (or Soda Core)
stack.kind: open-source (managed via GX Cloud / Soda Cloud)
stack.why: Declarative data-contract validations run as intake controls on inputs and as pre-release output verification, producing durable pass/fail evidence per run.

stack.name: Apache Kafka (with Schema Registry + DLQ)
stack.why: Authorizes sources via ACLs/mTLS, enforces schemas at ingest, and provides native dead-letter topics plus offsets for reconciliation of exactly-once delivery.

stack.name: Amazon S3 with Object Lock (WORM)
stack.why: Immutable, versioned, encrypted storage of inputs and outputs gives tamper-evident, durably protected retention that supports later reconciliation and audit.

capabilities.stack_notes: Pattern: Kafka+Schema Registry for authorized/validated intake and dead-letter, Temporal for exactly-once durable pipeline execution with retries/compensation, Great Expectations (or Soda) for intake and pre-release output verification, S3 Object Lock for WORM storage of inputs/outputs. dbt tests are a strong alternative to GX for batch/warehouse pipelines. GCP/Azure equivalents for WORM: GCS Bucket Lock, Azure Blob immutable storage. All confirmed current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: RBAC, Least Privilege & Identity Lifecycle
capabilities.description: Central identity provider with unique per-principal identities, a documented access-control policy, role-based least-privilege authorization, secure credential/secret handling, a joiner-mover-leaver provisioning flow with periodic recertification, elevated controls for privileged/break-glass accounts, and automatic access revocation on role change or termination.

stack.name: Microsoft Entra ID + Entra ID Governance (or Okta + Okta Identity Governance)
stack.why: Central cloud IdP giving each principal one identity with SSO/MFA and Conditional Access, plus built-in RBAC, joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle workflows and periodic access reviews/recertification.

stack.name: Keycloak
stack.why: Self-hosted OIDC/SAML identity provider alternative when you need to own the IdP: per-principal identities, realm/role-based authorization and fine-grained least-privilege policies.

stack.name: HashiCorp Vault (self-hosted or HCP Vault managed)
stack.why: Secure credential/secret handling with short-lived dynamic secrets, automatic rotation and tight lease-based least-privilege access to database and cloud credentials.

stack.name: Teleport
stack.why: Identity-aware access proxy for privileged/break-glass accounts: just-in-time elevation with approval, session recording, and automatic access revocation tied to IdP role changes or termination.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are widely adopted and current as of 2025-2026. Pick one primary IdP (managed Entra ID/Okta for fastest governance/recertification, or Keycloak if self-hosting is required) rather than both. Entra ID Governance / Okta Identity Governance cover the access-control policy, JML provisioning, recertification and automatic deprovisioning on termination; Vault covers secret handling; Teleport covers privileged/break-glass elevation and session audit. SCIM provisioning from the IdP to downstream apps ties revocation-on-role-change together end to end.

capabilities.name: Data Classification, Asset Inventory & Secure Data Lifecycle
capabilities.description: An owned asset/information inventory with a sensitivity classification and labelling scheme, acceptable-use and handling rules, encrypted and controlled transfer channels, asset return on offboarding, and verified data sanitization or secure destruction before equipment reuse, disposal, or off-site maintenance.

stack.name: Snipe-IT
stack.why: Widely-used IT asset/hardware inventory with per-asset ownership, custom sensitivity fields, and check-in/check-out that enforces asset return on offboarding.

stack.name: Microsoft Purview Information Protection
stack.why: De-facto sensitivity-labelling and classification scheme with attached encryption, acceptable-use/handling policy and DLP-enforced controlled transfer across data and endpoints.

stack.name: OpenMetadata
stack.why: Data-asset catalog that auto-classifies and tags datasets (PII/sensitivity), giving the inventory + labelling layer for structured data through its lifecycle.

stack.name: Blancco Drive Eraser
stack.why: Certified, verifiable data sanitization/destruction producing tamper-proof erasure certificates before equipment reuse, disposal, or off-site maintenance (NIST 800-88 / IEEE 2883).

capabilities.stack_notes: Open-source alternative for verified sanitization: nwipe/ShredOS (drive wiping) though it lacks Blancco's audit-grade certificates. Encrypted/controlled transfer channels are largely covered by the Purview DLP layer plus standard TLS/managed file-transfer; a dedicated MFT (e.g. GoAnywhere) can be added if regulated bulk transfers are in scope. All four confirmed current and actively maintained as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Cryptography: Encryption in Transit, At Rest & Key Management
capabilities.description: A documented cryptography policy enforcing strong current algorithms and adequate key lengths, TLS protection for all sensitive/personal data in transit (including service-to-service), encryption at rest for disks, databases and backups, and full-lifecycle management of keys, certificates and secrets (generation, storage, rotation, revocation, destruction) with tightly restricted access.

stack.name: HashiCorp Vault (or OpenBao)
stack.why: Central engine for the full key/secret lifecycle — generation, storage, automatic rotation, revocation and destruction — plus a built-in PKI CA, dynamic DB credentials, and tightly-scoped access policies enforcing the crypto standard.

stack.name: Cloud KMS / HSM (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, or Azure Key Vault Managed HSM)
stack.why: FIPS 140-2/3 hardware-backed root of trust for envelope encryption of disks, databases and backups, with auto-rotation and audited, IAM-restricted key access — the at-rest anchor Vault and services wrap their data keys against.

stack.name: cert-manager + Let's Encrypt/ACME
stack.why: Automates TLS certificate issuance, renewal and revocation across the platform so all sensitive/personal data in transit is protected without manual cert handling or expiry outages.

stack.name: Linkerd (or Istio) service mesh
stack.why: Transparently enforces mutual-TLS (modern ciphers, short-lived rotating certs) on every service-to-service call, closing the internal-traffic gap that edge TLS alone leaves open.

capabilities.stack_notes: Division of labor: Cloud KMS/HSM = hardware root of trust for at-rest envelope encryption; Vault/OpenBao = application-layer secrets, key lifecycle and internal PKI; cert-manager = edge/ingress TLS cert automation; service mesh = automatic service-to-service mTLS. Together they satisfy policy-enforced strong algorithms, transit protection (external + internal), at-rest for disks/DBs/backups, and full key/cert/secret lifecycle with restricted access. Infisical (available in this environment) is a lighter open-source/managed alternative to Vault if a Kubernetes-native, developer-friendly secrets store is preferred over Vault's broader PKI/dynamic-secrets feature set. All four are current and widely adopted as of 2026; OpenBao is the actively-maintained MPL fork of Vault worth choosing if BSL licensing is a concern.

capabilities.name: Network Segmentation & Multi-Tenant Isolation
capabilities.description: Secured and managed networks and devices, agreed security levels for in-house or outsourced network services, and traffic segregated into zones with logical per-tenant isolation in shared environments to limit lateral movement and contain compromise.

stack.name: Cilium (with Hubble)
stack.why: eBPF CNI that enforces identity-aware L3-L7 network policies and per-namespace/per-tenant isolation in Kubernetes, the de-facto standard for cloud-native segmentation with built-in flow observability.

stack.name: Istio Ambient Mesh
stack.why: Sidecar-less service mesh giving automatic mTLS and L7 authorization between workloads, creating zero-trust zones that contain lateral movement in shared multi-tenant clusters.

stack.name: Cloud VPC segmentation (AWS VPC / GCP VPC with subnets, security groups, and Network Firewall)
stack.why: Infrastructure-layer zoning — private subnets, security groups, and managed firewalls partition traffic into trust zones and set agreed security levels for in-house and outsourced services.

stack.name: Tailscale
stack.why: WireGuard-based zero-trust overlay with ACL-driven access for securely connecting managed devices and outsourced/third-party network services without exposing broad network reach.

capabilities.stack_notes: Assumes a Kubernetes-centric cloud-native greenfield build (the dominant 2026 pattern). Cilium + a mesh cover in-cluster per-tenant isolation and lateral-movement containment; VPC constructs handle infra-zone segregation; Tailscale covers secured device/service access. If not on Kubernetes, substitute Calico Enterprise or cloud-native microsegmentation (e.g., AWS security groups + PrivateLink) accordingly. All four confirmed current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026; no web search performed since these are well-established, actively maintained projects.

capabilities.name: Secure Remote Access & Egress Filtering
capabilities.description: Remote and administrative access occurs only over authenticated, encrypted channels (VPN or equivalent) rather than exposed plaintext services, and outbound web access from managed systems is filtered to reduce exposure to malicious or unauthorized sites.

stack.name: Tailscale
stack.why: WireGuard-based mesh VPN with identity-based ACLs and MFA, giving all remote access authenticated, encrypted, zero-plaintext-exposure connectivity without opening inbound ports.

stack.name: Teleport
stack.why: Identity-aware access proxy for SSH/Kubernetes/databases so administrative access runs over short-lived-cert, encrypted, fully audited channels instead of exposed services.

stack.name: Cloudflare Zero Trust (Gateway / Secure Web Gateway)
stack.why: DNS- and HTTP-layer egress filtering with category/threat blocklists for managed systems, plus ZTNA app access, reducing outbound exposure to malicious or unauthorized sites.

stack.name: Pomerium
stack.why: Self-hostable identity-aware reverse proxy for context-aware access to internal admin apps over TLS, a fully open alternative when a managed ZTNA is not desired.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. Tailscale + Cloudflare Zero Trust together cleanly cover both halves (encrypted remote access + egress web filtering); Teleport adds privileged-admin access with audit; Pomerium is an optional fully open-source ZTNA alternative. WireGuard is the open-source protocol baseline underneath Tailscale if a self-managed VPN is preferred. Recommend 3 as the core set (Tailscale, Teleport, Cloudflare Zero Trust) with Pomerium as the open-source substitute.

capabilities.name: Network Activity Monitoring & Anomaly Detection
capabilities.description: Network activity is continuously monitored and logged so anomalous or unauthorized traffic and security events can be detected, alerted on, and investigated.

stack.name: Suricata
stack.why: High-throughput IDS/IPS network sensor doing deep packet inspection and signature/rule-based alerting on suspicious or unauthorized traffic.

stack.name: Zeek
stack.why: Network security monitor that emits rich per-connection/protocol logs, the raw telemetry needed to detect anomalies and drive investigations.

stack.name: AWS GuardDuty
stack.why: Cloud-native ML threat detection over VPC Flow Logs, DNS, and CloudTrail — continuous anomaly/threat alerting with zero sensor operation.

stack.name: Elastic Security (SIEM)
stack.why: Ingests network + host logs, runs detection rules and ML anomaly jobs, and provides the alerting and investigation workflow on top of Suricata/Zeek output.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted in 2025-2026. Typical greenfield pattern: Suricata + Zeek as the on-network sensors feeding Elastic Security as the SIEM/detection-and-response layer; GuardDuty covers the cloud/VPC control-plane side natively for AWS-based builds (swap for Azure Sentinel / Google SCC on other clouds). Wazuh is a viable open-source SIEM alternative to Elastic Security if a lighter, agent-centric stack is preferred.

capabilities.name: Physical & Environmental Facility Security
capabilities.description: Physical safeguards for equipment and workspaces: clear-desk/clear-screen enforcement, secure equipment siting and screen-privacy positioning, protection against environmental threats, resilient supporting utilities, secured and segregated power/data cabling, and controlled authorized equipment maintenance.

stack.name: AWS Artifact / Google Cloud Compliance Reports / Azure Service Trust Portal (cloud provider physical-security inheritance)
stack.why: A greenfield build hosted in a hyperscaler inherits secure equipment siting, environmental threat protection, resilient utilities (redundant power/HVAC/fire), and controlled maintenance from the provider's SOC2/ISO27001-audited data centers — these portals give you the attestations to cite the inherited controls.

stack.name: Microsoft Intune (or Kandji / Jamf) MDM
stack.why: Enforces clear-screen technically via mandatory screen-lock/auto-timeout, encryption, and privacy policies pushed to every endpoint — the one part of this control that is directly software-enforceable rather than facility-based.

stack.name: NetBox
stack.why: The de-facto DCIM/IPAM system of record for documenting rack elevation, equipment siting, power feeds, and physical cabling with power/data segregation — the auditable source for cabling-security and secure-siting evidence in any owned or colo facility.

stack.name: Verkada (or Envoy for visitor management + Kisi for access control)
stack.why: Cloud-managed badge access control, environmental sensors (temp/humidity/leak/smoke), and visitor sign-in that governs authorized-only equipment maintenance and monitors environmental threats — needed only if you operate your own office/facility rather than pure cloud.

capabilities.stack_notes: This capability is overwhelmingly facility/hardware-based; for a pure-cloud greenfield build most of it (siting, environmental protection, utilities, cabling, maintenance) is inherited from the hosting provider and evidenced via their compliance portals rather than implemented in your own software. The only directly software-enforceable slice is clear-screen (MDM). NetBox and a physical-access/environmental-monitoring platform (Verkada/Envoy/Kisi) apply only if the org runs its own offices or colo space. All named tools are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026; no web search was needed to confirm.

capabilities.name: Endpoint & Off-Premises Asset Protection
capabilities.description: Devices and assets used, transported, or stored off-premises are protected against the higher risks of operating outside controlled facilities; off-site removal of equipment, information, or software requires prior authorization and tracking; and users safeguard unattended equipment via session termination, screen locks, and log-off.

stack.name: Microsoft Intune
stack.why: Cross-platform UEM/MDM that enforces full-disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault), idle screen-lock and auto-logoff policies, and remote lock/wipe for lost or off-premises devices.

stack.name: Jamf Pro
stack.why: Apple-fleet MDM that mandates FileVault, password-protected screen-saver locks, and remote lock/wipe — the standard for managing off-premises Mac/iOS assets.

stack.name: Fleet (osquery)
stack.why: Cross-platform device management and inventory that continuously verifies disk-encryption and lock-screen posture and flags non-compliant machines at scale.

stack.name: Snipe-IT
stack.why: IT asset-management system whose check-out/check-in workflow provides the prior-authorization approval and audit trail required for off-site removal of equipment.

capabilities.stack_notes: Intune + Jamf cover the unattended-equipment controls (screen lock, session termination, auto-logoff) and encryption for the higher off-premises risk; pick one or run both for a mixed Windows/Apple fleet. Fleet adds vendor-neutral, open-source compliance verification of that posture. Snipe-IT handles the distinct off-site removal authorization and tracking requirement, which MDM tools do not cover. All four are widely adopted and actively maintained as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Security Incident Detection, Response & Forensics
capabilities.description: An incident-management program with defined roles and runbooks, a staff event-reporting channel, event triage/classification, documented containment-eradication-recovery-communication workflows, post-incident learning feeding control improvements, and legally-admissible evidence collection with chain-of-custody preservation.

stack.name: Wazuh
stack.why: Open-source SIEM/XDR that ingests host and cloud telemetry to detect, correlate, and classify security events into triaged alerts.

stack.name: TheHive (with Cortex)
stack.why: Incident-response case management for triage/classification, runbook-driven CERT workflows, observable analysis, and post-incident review feeding control improvements.

stack.name: incident.io
stack.why: Managed incident orchestration providing the staff reporting channel, defined roles/on-call, and containment-recovery-communication coordination with automatic timelines.

stack.name: Velociraptor
stack.why: DFIR endpoint-forensics platform for evidence collection, live hunting, and artifact preservation supporting chain-of-custody for legally-admissible evidence.

capabilities.stack_notes: Coverage map: Wazuh = detection + event triage/classification; TheHive+Cortex = incident program, runbooks, post-incident learning; incident.io = reporting channel, roles, containment/eradication/recovery/communication workflows (PagerDuty or FireHydrant are equivalent managed alternatives); Velociraptor = forensics + chain-of-custody evidence collection. All confirmed current and actively maintained as of 2025-2026 from prior knowledge; no web search needed. Elastic Security or CrowdStrike Falcon are common managed substitutes for the detection layer.

capabilities.name: Vulnerability Remediation in the Delivery Pipeline
capabilities.description: Security vulnerabilities discovered during design, coding, testing, or acceptance are identified and remediated before systems are promoted to production.

stack.name: Trivy (Aqua Security)
stack.why: Single scanner covers dependencies, container images, IaC, and secrets; runs as a CI gate that fails the pipeline on HIGH/CRITICAL so nothing vulnerable is promoted.

stack.name: GitHub Advanced Security (CodeQL + Dependabot)
stack.why: Native SAST code scanning plus Dependabot alerts and automated fix pull requests, gating merges on the default branch before release.

stack.name: Snyk
stack.why: Continuous SCA/SAST/container/IaC scanning with one-click and automated remediation PRs, prioritizing reachable/exploitable issues to drive fixes pre-production.

stack.name: OWASP Dependency-Track
stack.why: SBOM-driven vulnerability management layer that continuously re-evaluates released and in-flight components against new CVEs and enforces policy gates for promotion.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. Typical greenfield pairing: Trivy or Snyk for the in-pipeline scan gate, GitHub Advanced Security/Dependabot for VCS-native code + dependency remediation, and Dependency-Track as the central SBOM/CVE tracking and policy layer. Choose the managed (Snyk/GHAS) vs open-source (Trivy/Dependency-Track) mix based on team size and budget; two well-integrated tools are usually sufficient rather than all four.

capabilities.name: Secure Development Lifecycle & Secure Coding
capabilities.description: Documented secure-development rules spanning the full lifecycle: security requirements specified for built or acquired apps, secure architecture and engineering principles applied, secure coding standards and tooling used, and security testing verifying requirements before release.

stack.name: OWASP ASVS 5.0 (Application Security Verification Standard)
stack.why: Gives you a versionable checklist of security requirements and secure-architecture controls to specify per app and verify before release.

stack.name: Semgrep
stack.why: SAST that enforces secure-coding standards as custom rules directly in CI/pre-commit, blocking insecure patterns at the developer's keyboard (managed Semgrep AppSec Platform also available).

stack.name: GitHub Advanced Security (CodeQL + secret scanning + Dependabot)
stack.why: One integrated managed layer for deep SAST, secret detection, and dependency/SCA scanning gating pull requests before merge.

stack.name: OWASP ZAP
stack.why: DAST that runs automated security tests against the running app in CI to verify runtime security requirements before a release ships.

capabilities.stack_notes: These are stable, widely-adopted choices for 2025-2026. Open-source alternatives if avoiding GitHub's managed suite: Trivy (SCA/IaC/container scanning) plus Gitleaks or TruffleHog (secret scanning). Snyk is the common commercial equivalent to GHAS. ASVS is a standard rather than a running tool, but it is the load-bearing artifact for the requirements/architecture stages of this capability; the three scanners cover secure-coding and pre-release testing.

capabilities.name: Change & Release Management for Production
capabilities.description: Changes to systems and information-processing facilities follow formal change management (assessment, approval, testing, rollback), and installation/updating of software on operational systems is governed so only approved, authorized software reaches production.

stack.name: GitHub (Enterprise) — PRs + required reviewers + Environment protection rules
stack.why: Formal change management gate in code: pull-request approvals, CODEOWNERS, and per-environment required reviewers/wait timers give every production change assessment, sign-off, and an immutable audit trail (GitLab is the open-source equivalent).

stack.name: Argo CD
stack.why: CNCF-graduated GitOps delivery: Git is the single source of truth so only merged/approved manifests reach production, with declarative diff, drift detection, and one-click rollback to any prior revision.

stack.name: Argo Rollouts
stack.why: Progressive delivery (canary / blue-green) with metric-based analysis and automated rollback, satisfying the testing-in-production and safe-revert parts of the control.

stack.name: Kyverno + Sigstore Cosign
stack.why: Kubernetes admission policies that verify image signatures/attestations and enforce provenance, so only signed, authorized software is admitted to the cluster (governs installation/updates to operational systems).

capabilities.stack_notes: Pattern: change approval in Git (GitHub/GitLab) -> GitOps deploy (Argo CD) -> progressive rollout+rollback (Argo Rollouts) -> admission-time authorization of only signed images (Kyverno+Cosign). OPA Gatekeeper is an alternative to Kyverno; Flagger an alternative to Argo Rollouts (esp. with Flux instead of Argo CD). All are current, widely-adopted CNCF projects as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Environment Separation & Test Data Protection
capabilities.description: Development, test, and production environments are separated with controlled promotion; production/sensitive data is not used in test unless masked, anonymized, or otherwise safeguarded and authorized; and audit access to operational systems is planned and controlled to minimize production impact.

stack.name: Argo CD
stack.why: GitOps controller enforces separated dev/test/prod environments with reviewed, promotion-gated deploys (each env a distinct app/target), giving auditable controlled promotion.

stack.name: OpenTofu (with per-environment workspaces/state)
stack.why: Infrastructure-as-code with isolated state per environment cleanly separates dev/test/prod resources and networks so environments never share live infrastructure by accident.

stack.name: Neosync
stack.why: Purpose-built data anonymization/synthetic-data platform that masks and subsets production data before it lands in test, so sensitive prod data is never used unmasked.

stack.name: Teleport
stack.why: Identity-aware access proxy for prod databases/servers/k8s with RBAC, short-lived certs, approval workflows and full session recording — planned, controlled, audited operational access.

capabilities.stack_notes: Coverage maps to the three requirements: Argo CD + OpenTofu = separated environments with controlled promotion; Neosync = masked/anonymized test data instead of raw production data; Teleport = planned, controlled, audited access to operational systems. All four are widely adopted in 2025-2026. Managed alternatives if a hosted service is preferred: Tonic.ai (data masking) in place of Neosync, and StrongDM/Teleport Cloud for audited prod access. Confidence is high on currency/adoption; no web search was performed.

capabilities.name: Supplier, ICT Supply-Chain & Cloud Security Management
capabilities.description: A vendor risk-management process with due diligence before and during engagement, security requirements embedded in supplier agreements and flowed down through the ICT/software-component supply chain, continuous monitoring and change management of supplier services, and cloud-service governance covering acquisition, shared-responsibility boundaries, and secure exit.

stack.name: OneTrust Third-Party Risk Management
stack.why: Runs the vendor lifecycle end-to-end — intake, due-diligence assessments, risk scoring, contract/security-requirement flow-down, and reassessment workflows — the widely-adopted TPRM system of record.

stack.name: Bitsight (or SecurityScorecard)
stack.why: Continuous outside-in security ratings that monitor each supplier's posture between assessments and alert on material changes across the ICT supply chain.

stack.name: OWASP Dependency-Track
stack.why: Ingests supplier/first-party SBOMs (CycloneDX) to track software-component risk and flow-down obligations down the software supply chain, with continuous CVE/VEX alerting.

stack.name: Wiz (or open-source Prowler)
stack.why: Cloud-service governance and CSPM — enforces shared-responsibility boundaries, misconfiguration/exposure detection, and inventory needed for secure cloud acquisition and exit.

capabilities.stack_notes: Coverage maps to the four sub-capabilities: OneTrust = due diligence + contractual security requirements + change management; Bitsight/SecurityScorecard = continuous supplier monitoring; Dependency-Track = ICT/software-component supply-chain flow-down via SBOMs; Wiz/Prowler = cloud governance, shared-responsibility boundaries, and secure exit. Pair Dependency-Track with Syft/Grype (open-source, Anchore) if SBOM generation and scanning are also needed. Managed ratings vendors (Bitsight vs SecurityScorecard) and CSPM (Wiz vs Prowler) are interchangeable per budget — the open-source alternative is noted for the cloud-governance slot.

capabilities.name: Outsourced Development Oversight
capabilities.description: Third-party and outsourced development activity is directed, monitored, and reviewed so the organization's security requirements are met throughout the engagement.

stack.name: GitHub Enterprise (CODEOWNERS + branch protection + required reviews + audit log)
stack.why: Directs and reviews every outsourced contribution: mandatory code owner review, protected branches, and a full audit log of who changed what.

stack.name: Vanta
stack.why: TPRM/vendor security module tracks each development vendor's security posture, contracts, and continuous review so requirements are enforced through the engagement.

stack.name: Semgrep
stack.why: Policy-as-code SAST/secrets scanning gate on outsourced-developer PRs so third-party code must meet your security rules before merge.

stack.name: Sigstore / cosign (with SLSA provenance)
stack.why: Signs and verifies build provenance of artifacts produced by outsourced pipelines, proving what shipped came from a trusted, reviewed source.

capabilities.stack_notes: Focus is oversight of third-party/outsourced dev: GitHub Enterprise governs and records the contribution flow (direct + review), Vanta covers the vendor-risk/monitoring side, Semgrep enforces security requirements on incoming code, and Sigstore/cosign verifies provenance of outsourced build outputs. All are widely adopted and current as of 2025-2026. GitHub Advanced Security or Snyk are viable swaps for Semgrep; Drata or OneTrust for Vanta.

capabilities.name: PII/Privacy Controls & Legal-Regulatory Register
capabilities.description: PII-aware data handling (privacy-by-design safeguards, PII discovery/tagging, consent and retention enforcement), a maintained register of applicable legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual obligations mapped to controls, and intellectual-property/software-licensing compliance tracking.

stack.name: Microsoft Presidio
stack.why: Self-hostable PII discovery, tagging, and de-identification (mask/hash/redact) across text, images, and structured data — the privacy-by-design safeguard you embed directly in data pipelines and LLM guardrails; actively released through 2026 (MIT).

stack.name: Transcend
stack.why: Middleware-layer consent management plus DSAR and data-retention/deletion enforcement across every system and region — automates consent capture and retention policy so privacy obligations are enforced, not just documented.

stack.name: Vanta
stack.why: GRC/trust-management platform that maintains the register of applicable legal, regulatory and contractual obligations mapped to controls with continuous evidence collection across GDPR, SOC 2, and ISO 27001 frameworks.

stack.name: OSS Review Toolkit (ORT)
stack.why: Linux Foundation toolkit that scans dependencies across 20+ package managers for license/IP obligations, enforces policy, and generates SPDX/CycloneDX SBOMs — covers the intellectual-property and software-licensing compliance leg (FOSSA is the managed alternative).

capabilities.stack_notes: Chosen to cover the three distinct sub-domains of this capability: (1) PII-aware data handling = Presidio; (2) consent + retention enforcement = Transcend; (3) obligations-register-mapped-to-controls = Vanta; (4) IP/software-licensing = ORT. All four verified current as of 2026 via web search. Substitution notes: OneTrust is the higher-mindshare (17.3% DPMS) but heavier alternative to Transcend and can also serve as the obligations register if you prefer one privacy suite over Vanta; Drata is an equivalent managed GRC alternative to Vanta; FOSSA/Black Duck are managed alternatives to ORT with stronger license-edge-case databases. For a greenfield 2026 build, Presidio + ORT (open-source, embed-in-pipeline) plus one managed privacy platform (Transcend) and one managed GRC backbone (Vanta) balances engineering control against auditable, framework-mapped evidence.

capabilities.name: Security Governance, HR Security & Operating Procedures
capabilities.description: Documented operating procedures for information-processing facilities plus the people-side program: pre-employment screening, security responsibilities in employment terms, recurring awareness training, a graduated disciplinary process, signed confidentiality/NDA agreements, remote-working controls, and duties that survive termination or role change.

stack.name: Vanta
stack.why: GRC platform that centralizes SOC2/ISO27001/GDPR programs: manages policy publishing and employee acknowledgment (security responsibilities, confidentiality), tracks recurring awareness training and background-check completion, and enforces onboarding/offboarding duties that survive termination.

stack.name: KnowBe4
stack.why: Market-leading security awareness training and phishing-simulation platform for the recurring training program, with per-user risk scoring that feeds a graduated disciplinary process; actively shipping in 2026 (AIDA orchestration, HRM analytics).

stack.name: Checkr
stack.why: Widely-adopted pre-employment background screening API/service (identity, criminal, employment verification) that satisfies the personnel-screening control and integrates cleanly with HRIS and GRC tools like Vanta.

stack.name: BookStack
stack.why: Self-hosted, version-controlled documentation wiki for the documented operating procedures for information-processing facilities, giving reviewable, page-level-permissioned SOPs and remote-working guidelines without vendor lock-in.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four verified current for 2025-2026. Vanta and KnowBe4 both have active 2026 product releases (Vanta multi-source training assignment; KnowBe4 AIDA phishing orchestration). Division of labor: Vanta = policy/acknowledgment/training-tracking/offboarding governance layer; KnowBe4 = actual awareness-training content + phishing + disciplinary risk signal; Checkr = pre-employment screening; BookStack = the SOP/operating-procedure documentation itself. Alternatives worth noting: Drata or Secureframe substitute for Vanta; Hoxhunt or Curricula substitute for KnowBe4; Certn substitutes for Checkr; GitBook, Notion, or Confluence substitute for BookStack if a managed docs tool is preferred over self-hosting. Counterparty NDA e-signing (vs. internal policy acknowledgment, which Vanta covers) would need a signature tool like DocuSign if that is in scope.

capabilities.name: ICT Continuity & Disaster Recovery
capabilities.description: Backup, redundancy and failover capabilities with defined RTO/RPO targets, plus documented and regularly tested restore procedures so information and systems can be recovered to meet business-continuity objectives.

stack.name: AWS Backup
stack.why: Policy-driven centralized backups across AWS services with cross-region/cross-account copy and built-in restore testing to enforce RTO/RPO.

stack.name: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
stack.why: Continuous block-level replication with automated failover/failback and low-cost staging, giving measurable minutes-scale RTO for whole workloads.

stack.name: Velero
stack.why: CNCF-standard Kubernetes backup and cross-cluster restore of cluster state plus persistent volumes, enabling regional failover of containerized apps.

stack.name: pgBackRest
stack.why: Reliable PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery with parallel, incremental, encrypted backups to object storage to hit tight database RPO targets.

capabilities.stack_notes: Layered coverage: DRS for VM/server-level failover, Velero for Kubernetes, pgBackRest for database PITR, AWS Backup as the governing backup/restore-test policy plane. All are widely adopted and current as of 2025-2026. Cloud-agnostic swaps if not on AWS: Azure Site Recovery / Google Backup and DR for the managed pieces; restic or Kopia as an open-source general-purpose backup engine. Whichever stack is chosen, the compliance requirement demands scheduled restore drills and documented RTO/RPO per system, not just backup configuration.
